nodes.title: Level 0 overview: Software Engineering Fundamentals
nodes.summary: Level 0 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: become comfortable building, debugging, and deploying real software before adding LLMs. This is the engineering foundation for everything that follows.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (9/10): Many AI engineer roles screen candidates as software engineers first, with coding rounds, backend questions, and API design. If you fail these, you never reach the AI rounds.

Why it matters on the job (10/10): Most of the work is regular software engineering: APIs, databases, testing, debugging, deployments. Most production incidents are ordinary software bugs, not model problems.
Prerequisites: Nothing — this is the start

Goal of this level: Level 0 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: become comfortable building, debugging, and deploying real software before adding LLMs. This is the engineering foundation for everything that follows.
Plan 7 modules and the capstone “Ship a No-AI REST Service” before moving on

nodes.title: M0.1 · Python for AI Engineering
nodes.summary: M0.1 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 12 topics: Clean, idiomatic Python; Core data structures; Type hints & typed models.
checklist: Clean, idiomatic Python: Write clean, idiomatic Python using functions, classes, modules, comprehensions, exceptions, and common standard-library utilities.
Core data structures: Reason confidently about core data structures: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, iterators, generators, and when to use each.
Type hints & typed models: Use type hints, dataclass/Pydantic-style models, and static analysis to make interfaces explicit and catch mistakes earlier.
Mutability, scope & failure modes: Understand mutability, references, scope, exceptions, context managers, and common Python failure modes.
Files, paths, env vars & serialization: Work with files, paths, environment variables, JSON, CSV, and basic serialization.
Sync vs async execution: Understand synchronous vs asynchronous execution; use async / await to perform concurrent network/API calls without blocking.
Environments & dependencies with uv: Manage virtual environments and dependencies with uv; understand pyproject.toml, dependency locking, and reproducible environments.
Modules & packages: Structure larger programs into modules and packages instead of writing everything in one script.
Unit tests and debugging: Write basic unit tests with pytest and learn to debug using stack traces, logs, and breakpoints.
Logging vs print for production services: Prefer structured logging over print so request ids and errors are searchable.
Virtualenv vs uv lockfile discipline: Reproduce a teammate's environment from the lockfile, not from memory.
Interview: debug a failing pytest: Walk through reading the traceback, isolating the unit, and writing a regression test.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.1: Python for AI Engineering (source)

nodes.title: M0.2 · The Web: HTTP, REST & JSON
nodes.summary: M0.2 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 11 topics: The HTTP request/response cycle; Methods & idempotency; Status codes.
checklist: The HTTP request/response cycle: Understand the full HTTP request/response cycle: URL, method, headers, body, server processing, response, and status code.
Methods & idempotency: Work with common methods such as GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, and DELETE, and understand idempotency at a practical level.
Status codes: Understand important status-code families and common codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, and 500.
Headers, params, bodies & cookies: Understand headers, query parameters, path parameters, request bodies, content types, and cookies at a practical level.
Working with JSON: Produce, parse, validate, and manipulate JSON confidently.
RESTful resource design: Understand RESTful resource design and design clean endpoints for a simple application.
Authentication basics: Understand authentication basics: API keys, bearer tokens, authorization headers, and why secrets should not be embedded in URLs or client code.
Inspecting APIs with curl & Postman: Use tools such as curl, Postman/Bruno, or Python HTTP clients to inspect and debug APIs.
Pagination, filtering and idempotency keys: Design list endpoints that clients can retry without creating duplicates.
Content negotiation and error bodies: Return a consistent JSON error shape with a code, message and request id.
Interview: design a tiny REST resource: Sketch verbs, status codes and what 409 vs 422 means for that resource.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.2: The Web: HTTP, REST & JSON (source)

nodes.title: M0.3 · Building APIs with FastAPI
nodes.summary: M0.3 in Level 0 (Software Engineering Fundamentals), 10 topics: Routes, parameters & response models; Validation with Pydantic; Dependency injection.
checklist: Routes, parameters & response models: Build a FastAPI application with routes, path/query parameters, request bodies, and response models.
Validation with Pydantic: Use Pydantic models for validation, serialization, typed inputs, and typed outputs.
Dependency injection: Understand dependency injection at a practical level for reusable application dependencies.
Status codes & error responses: Return appropriate HTTP status codes and design consistent error responses.
Clean exception handling: Handle exceptions cleanly instead of leaking raw stack traces to clients.
Generated OpenAPI docs: Use FastAPI's automatically generated OpenAPI/Swagger documentation and understand how API schemas are derived.
Sync vs async endpoints: Write synchronous and asynchronous endpoints and understand when each is appropriate.
Calling external services without blocking: Call external HTTP services from async endpoints without blocking the server.
Startup, config & middleware: Understand application startup/shutdown, configuration through environment variables, and basic middleware concepts.
Testing endpoints: Test endpoints using pytest and FastAPI's test client.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.3: Building APIs with FastAPI (source)

nodes.title: M0.4 · Data & Persistence Basics
nodes.summary: M0.4 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 10 topics: Relational data modeling; SQL with PostgreSQL; Indexes & query performance.
checklist: Relational data modeling: Understand relational data modeling: tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, relationships, and basic normalization.
SQL with PostgreSQL: Use PostgreSQL and write SQL for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, filtering, sorting, grouping, joins, and basic aggregations.
Indexes & query performance: Understand indexes conceptually and why query design affects performance.
Connecting a database to the app: Connect PostgreSQL to a Python/FastAPI application using a database driver or ORM.
Credentials outside source code: Keep database credentials outside source code and manage configuration through environment variables.
Migrations as versioned schema: Treat schema changes as reviewed artefacts that can roll forward, never edit production by hand.
Transactions and isolation in practice: Know when a write needs a transaction and what happens if two requests update the same row.
ORMs vs raw SQL: Use an ORM for routine CRUD and drop to SQL when you need an EXPLAIN or a tight join.
Connection pooling: Reuse connections instead of opening one per request; size the pool for the worker count.
Interview: model a simple orders schema: Sketch users, orders and line items with keys and one index you would add first.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.4: Data & Persistence Basics (source)

nodes.title: M0.5 · Git & Collaboration
nodes.summary: M0.5 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 10 topics: Repos, commits, branches & remotes; The branch → PR → merge workflow; Commit messages & history.
checklist: Repos, commits, branches & remotes: Understand repositories, commits, branches, remotes, diffs, and the staging area.
The branch → PR → merge workflow: Follow a practical workflow: branch → make changes → commit → push → pull request → review → merge.
Commit messages & history: Write useful commit messages and inspect history using Git tools.
Resolving merge conflicts: Resolve merge conflicts confidently rather than avoiding them.
Keeping secrets out with .gitignore: Understand .gitignore and prevent secrets, virtual environments, generated files, and local configuration from entering the repository.
Writing a README: Write a README that explains what the project does, how to install it, configure it, run it, test it, and call its API.
Code review & protected branches: Understand basic collaboration concepts such as code review, pull requests, and protected main branches.
Rewriting shared history is not allowed: Never force-push a branch others pulled; revert or add a fix commit instead.
Bisect to find a regression: Use git bisect when a bug appeared between two known-good commits.
Interview: walk a PR you would reject: Name a missing test, a secret, or an unclear commit and what you would ask for.

nodes.title: M0.6 · AI-Assisted Software Development
nodes.summary: M0.6 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 16 topics: Autocomplete → assistants → agents; AI-assisted engineering vs vibe coding; Explore, implement & debug with an agent.
checklist: [Agentic coding fundamentals] Autocomplete → assistants → agents: Understand the progression from autocomplete, to chat-based assistants, to coding agents that can read a repository, edit code, run commands, inspect the results, and iterate.

[Agentic coding fundamentals] AI-assisted engineering vs vibe coding: Distinguish AI-assisted engineering, where you direct and verify the work, from blind vibe coding, where you accept whatever is generated.

[Agentic coding fundamentals] Explore, implement & debug with an agent: Use a coding agent such as Claude Code to explore an unfamiliar repository, implement targeted changes, and debug existing code.
[Agentic coding fundamentals] The verification loop: Work the verification loop on every change: give context → generate → inspect the Git diff → test → debug → review → accept.
[Context, CLAUDE.md & planning] Minimum useful context: Understand the finite context window and give the minimum useful context for a task instead of pointing the agent at the entire repository.

[Context, CLAUDE.md & planning] CLAUDE.md as project memory: Keep architecture, conventions, project commands, and testing instructions in a project instruction file such as CLAUDE.md, separate from temporary task context.

[Context, CLAUDE.md & planning] Spec-driven development & planning: Practice spec-driven development: write the requirement and the specification, then review a plan before the agent changes the repository.

[Reusable workflows: commands & Skills] Slash commands & Skills: Turn prompts you retype into custom slash commands, and understand Skills as reusable capabilities with instructions, metadata, and examples that load only when needed.
[Reusable workflows: commands & Skills] Skills worth building: Build skills for recurring work such as code review, test generation, documentation, refactoring, and repository-specific conventions.

[Subagents & external tools] Delegating to subagents: Delegate specialized work to subagents such as a reviewer, tester, debugger, or researcher instead of forcing every responsibility into one context.

[Subagents & external tools] External systems through MCP: Connect the agent to systems outside the repository through MCP (Model Context Protocol): databases, APIs, developer tools, and documentation.
[Hooks, plugins & the professional loop] Hooks for deterministic checks: Use hooks to make formatting, linting, testing, and validation deterministic instead of asking a model to remember them.
[Hooks, plugins & the professional loop] Plugins as capability bundles: Understand plugins as reusable bundles that package commands, skills, hooks, agents, and integrations together.

[Hooks, plugins & the professional loop] Skills that transfer across agents: Understand that these skills transfer to any coding agent — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI — because the durable parts are context, specifications, planning, delegation, automation, and verification.
Reviewing AI-generated diffs: Treat model output as an untrusted PR: tests, secrets, and edge cases before merge.
Prompting the assistant with failing tests: Give the model the traceback and the intended assertion, not a vague 'fix it'.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.6: AI-Assisted Software Development (source)

nodes.title: M0.7 · Capstone: Ship a No-AI REST Service
nodes.summary: M0.7 in L0 · Software Engineering Fundamentals, 10 topics: App vs environment vs machine; Containers & images; Writing and running a Dockerfile.
checklist: App vs environment vs machine: Understand the practical distinction between your application, its environment, and the machine running it.
Containers & images: Understand containers and images conceptually and why Docker improves reproducibility.
Writing and running a Dockerfile: Write a Dockerfile, build an image, run a container locally, expose ports, and pass environment variables safely.
Layers, logs & startup failures: Understand image layers, .dockerignore, container logs, and common container startup failures.
Containerizing a FastAPI app: Containerize a FastAPI application and connect it to its required configuration/services.
Deploying to a public URL: Deploy a service to a cloud/platform provider and expose it through a publicly reachable URL.
Production env vars & secrets: Configure production environment variables and secrets separately from local development.
Health checks and readiness: Expose liveness vs readiness so the platform does not send traffic to a booting app.
Image tags vs latest: Pin digest or a version tag; latest is not reproducible.
Interview: debug a container that exits 1: Read logs, check the CMD, env vars and whether the port is bound.

links.title: Level 0 module M0.7: Capstone: Ship a No-AI REST Service (source)

nodes.title: Capstone · Ship a No-AI REST Service
nodes.summary: Ship it: the Level 0 capstone. Ship it · Level 0 capstone. Build it, publish it, and be ready to explain every decision.
checklist: The full no-AI stack: Build a complete application using Python + FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Git + Docker + deployment, with no LLM or AI dependency.
Choosing a realistic domain: Design a small but realistic domain such as task management, bookmarks, expense tracking, inventory, notes, or support tickets.
REST endpoints with persistent CRUD: Implement multiple REST endpoints with validated request/response schemas and persistent CRUD operations.
An external API integration: Include at least one external API integration and use async execution where appropriate.
Handling every failure path: Handle validation failures, missing resources, external-service errors, and unexpected server errors cleanly.
Tests, config & logging: Add basic automated tests, configuration via environment variables, and useful application logging.
Clean repo and README: Maintain the project in Git with a clean repository structure and a README containing setup and usage instructions.
Docker packaging & deployment: Package the service with Docker and deploy it to a publicly reachable URL.
Verifying the deployed API: Verify the deployed API using its OpenAPI docs, curl, or an API client.
Coding agent during the build: Use a coding agent for meaningful parts of the build; "no-AI" means the deployed product needs no LLM, not that you code without AI tools.
Diff review before accepting: Review every meaningful generated change through its Git diff before accepting it.
Validating generated code: Validate generated code through tests, type checking, linting, logs, and manual API calls.
Explain it without the agent: Explain the architecture and the important code paths yourself, without asking the coding agent.

Document one AI failure: Document one case where the coding agent produced an incorrect, incomplete, insecure, over-engineered, or otherwise suboptimal solution: what it proposed, why it was wrong, how you detected it, what you changed, and the engineering lesson you took from it.

nodes.title: Level 1 overview: LLM 101
nodes.summary: Level 1 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Build a strong mental model of how LLMs work, why they behave the way they do, and how to choose and use the right model for a task.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (8/10): Conceptual questions are very common in screening rounds: tokens, attention, temperature, hallucination, context limits. Shaky answers here end the interview early, because they suggest you’ve only used LLMs, not understood them.
Why it matters on the job (7/10): It shapes good decisions about cost, latency, and model behaviour, and helps you debug odd outputs. But you use it as background knowledge, not every day.
Prerequisites: None
Goal of this level: Level 1 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Build a strong mental model of how LLMs work, why they behave the way they do, and how to choose and use the right model for a task.
Plan 12 modules before moving on

links.title: 100 Days of AI Engineering · LLM Fundamentals

nodes.title: M1.1 · What an LLM Actually Is
nodes.summary: M1.1 in L1 · LLM 101, 8 topics: Next-token prediction; What an LLM is not; Why one model does many tasks.
checklist: Next-token prediction: Understand what a Large Language Model actually does, with next-token prediction as the core idea and generation as a repeated predict → choose → append → repeat process.
What an LLM is not: Understand what an LLM is not: a database, search engine, deterministic program, or repository of stored answers.
Why one model does many tasks: Understand why the same underlying model can perform writing, summarization, translation, coding, question answering, and classification.
Where capability comes from: Build intuition for how capability improves through better data, more compute, larger models, and better training.
Training data vs the weights you call: The API exposes a frozen function; it does not browse the web unless you add a tool.
Likelihood is not a database lookup: The model samples a continuation; it does not retrieve a stored sentence.
Scale, data and algorithms together: Capability comes from all three, not from 'just more parameters'.
Interview: what an LLM cannot do: Name tool use, fresh facts, and guaranteed arithmetic as things you add around the model.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.1: What an LLM Actually Is (source)

nodes.title: M1.2 · Tokenization
nodes.summary: M1.2 in L1 · LLM 101, 7 topics: Characters, words & tokens; Tokenizing across languages & code; Why tokens drive cost and latency.
checklist: Characters, words & tokens: Distinguish characters, words, and tokens; understand token IDs, why LLMs operate on tokens, and why different tokenizers can split the same text differently.
Tokenizing across languages & code: Explore tokenization of normal English, uncommon words, numbers, code, emojis, Hindi/Devanagari, and mixed Hindi-English text.

Why tokens drive cost and latency: Connect tokenization to API pricing, context-window consumption, output length, latency, spelling difficulties, character-counting failures, and mathematical/numerical behavior.
Special tokens and chat templates: Roles and stops are tokens too; a wrong template silently wrecks quality.
Tokenizers are model-specific: Never reuse another model's token ids or count; cost estimates will be wrong.
Subword surprises in code and numbers: A long number or identifier can explode into many tokens.
Interview: estimate tokens for a prompt: Count roughly 4 characters per token in English, then check with the real tokenizer.

nodes.title: M1.3 · Inside an LLM: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers
nodes.summary: M1.3 in L1 · LLM 101, 12 topics: From token IDs to embeddings; What parameter counts mean; Why bigger is not automatically better.
checklist: [Tokens → Vectors] From token IDs to embeddings: Understand how token IDs become embeddings, what vectors represent conceptually, why concepts are represented numerically, and how representations change as they pass through transformer layers.
[Tokens → Vectors] What parameter counts mean: Understand what model parameters are and what sizes such as 8B, 70B, and 400B+ mean.
[Tokens → Vectors] Why bigger is not automatically better: Understand why more parameters can increase capacity, while larger does not automatically mean better.
[Attention] The intuition behind attention: Understand attention through the intuition: a token looks at other relevant tokens in the context to build a better representation of what it means.

[Attention] Queries, keys, values & causal attention: Build a high-level understanding of queries, keys, values, attention scores, transformer layers, and causal attention — without matrix mathematics.
[Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts] Dense models: Understand a dense model, where every parameter takes part in producing every token.

[Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts] Mixture-of-Experts & routing: Understand a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, where the feed-forward layers are split into many experts and a router selects only a few of them for each token.

[Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts] Total vs active parameters: Distinguish total parameters from active parameters, and understand why an MoE model with a very large total size can cost far less to run than a dense model of the same size.

[Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts] What MoE changes in practice: Understand what MoE changes in practice: every expert still has to be held in memory, while the compute spent per token stays closer to that of a much smaller model.

[Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts] Reading MoE model cards: Read MoE descriptions on model cards, such as "8x7B" or "total vs active parameters", and know what they tell you about speed, cost, and hosting requirements.
Residual streams and layer stacking: Each block adds a residual update; depth is how the representation is refined.
Why positional information is required: Without position, the model cannot tell 'dog bites man' from the reverse.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.3: Inside an LLM: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers (source)

nodes.title: M1.4 · How LLMs Learn
nodes.summary: M1.4 in L1 · LLM 101, 9 topics: Pretraining & self-supervision; What pretraining teaches; Memorization vs generalization.
checklist: [Pretraining] Pretraining & self-supervision: Understand pretraining, how enormous text datasets are used, why next-token prediction creates its own training signal, and what self-supervised learning means.
[Pretraining] What pretraining teaches: Understand how pretraining enables models to learn grammar, facts, patterns, concepts, relationships, coding syntax, and problem-solving patterns.
[Pretraining] Memorization vs generalization: Explore memorization vs generalization, including why an LLM can sometimes answer questions it has never seen verbatim.
[Post-training] The post-training pipeline: Understand the broad pipeline: Pretraining → Supervised Fine-Tuning → Preference / Reinforcement Training → Deployed Assistant.
[Post-training] SFT, RLHF & preference optimization: Understand SFT, RLHF, RLAIF, preference optimization at a conceptual level, and safety tuning.

[Post-training] Why chat models behave as they do: Connect post-training to why chat models follow instructions, answer conversationally, refuse certain requests, hedge, structure answers, and ask for clarification.
Instruction following is post-trained: Base models complete text; chat behaviour is taught after pretraining.
Preference data quality beats volume: Noisy raters teach the model the wrong taste.
Interview: SFT vs RLHF in one minute: SFT teaches format; preference training teaches which of two answers is better.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.4: How LLMs Learn (source)

nodes.title: M1.5 · How LLM Inference Works
nodes.summary: M1.5 in L1 · LLM 101, 8 topics: What happens after you send a prompt; Prefill vs decode; Tokens, TTFT & total latency.
checklist: What happens after you send a prompt: Understand what happens after sending a prompt to an LLM API: Prompt → process input → predict token → generate token → repeat.
Prefill vs decode: Distinguish prefill, where the model processes the input/context, from decode, where new tokens are generated one by one.
Tokens, TTFT & total latency: Understand input tokens, output tokens, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and total latency.
KV caching: Build intuition for KV caching and why the model does not need to recompute the entire conversation from scratch after every generated token.
Why inference mechanics drive cost: Connect inference mechanics to latency, cost, long prompts, long outputs, and reasoning models.
Batching decode vs interactive TTFT: Throughput and first-token latency fight each other; pick for the product.
Speculative decoding at a glance: A cheap draft model proposes tokens a larger model verifies.
Interview: explain a slow first token: Prefill is compute-bound on the whole prompt; long context raises TTFT.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.5: How LLM Inference Works (source)

nodes.title: M1.6 · Sampling & Generation Parameters
nodes.summary: M1.6 in L1 · LLM 101, 8 topics: From probabilities to a chosen token; Temperature, top-p, top-k & penalties; Matching randomness to the task.
checklist: From probabilities to a chosen token: Start from the model's next-token probability distribution and ask: which token should actually be generated?
Temperature, top-p, top-k & penalties: Understand greedy decoding, temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum output tokens, stop sequences, and repetition/frequency/presence penalties where supported.

Matching randomness to the task: Understand task-dependent randomness: lower randomness for extraction, structured output, classification, and factual QA; higher randomness for brainstorming, creative writing, and diverse alternatives.
Differences across model APIs: Understand that different model APIs expose different controls and that some reasoning models provide less direct control over traditional sampling parameters.
Greedy decode vs sampling: Temperature 0 is not always deterministic across providers or batch sizes.
Repetition and frequency penalties: Use them for creative text, not for JSON or classification.
Seed and reproducibility limits: Seeds help debugging; they are not a correctness guarantee.
Interview: pick sampling for JSON: Low temperature, stop sequences, and a schema beat clever penalties.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.6: Sampling & Generation Parameters (source)

nodes.title: M1.7 · Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute
nodes.summary: M1.7 in L1 · LLM 101, 8 topics: Why some models think longer; Test-time compute & thinking budgets; Where reasoning helps.
checklist: Why some models think longer: Understand why some models spend substantially more compute before producing an answer.
Test-time compute & thinking budgets: Build intuition for test-time compute, reasoning effort, thinking budgets, and internal reasoning tokens/compute.
Where reasoning helps: Identify tasks where reasoning tends to help: difficult mathematics, complex coding, planning, multi-step logic, and constraint-heavy problems.
Where reasoning is unnecessary: Identify tasks where it may be unnecessary: sentiment classification, simple extraction, rewriting, and straightforward summarization.
The quality / cost / latency trade-off: Understand the trade-off: more reasoning can improve quality but generally increases cost and latency.

Prompting reasoning models: Adapt prompting for reasoning models: move away from relying on “think step by step” and instead clearly state the goal, provide relevant context, specify constraints, and define what a good answer looks like.
Budget tokens vs user-visible tokens: Hidden thinking can consume the max-output limit.
When to spend extra test-time compute: Hard multi-step problems; not extraction or rewrite.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.7: Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute (source)

nodes.title: M1.8 · The Context Window
nodes.summary: M1.8 in L1 · LLM 101, 7 topics: What occupies the context window; Context ≠ knowledge ≠ memory; What goes wrong in long contexts.
checklist: What occupies the context window: Understand what the context window is and what can occupy it: system instructions, conversation history, user prompts, documents, examples, tool outputs, and generated content.
Context ≠ knowledge ≠ memory: Distinguish context ≠ model knowledge ≠ long-term memory.
What goes wrong in long contexts: Understand what can happen with very long contexts: truncation, attention degradation, lost-in-the-middle effects, and context dilution.
Why a big window is not enough: Understand why a model supporting a huge context window does not mean it can use every token equally well.
Prompt, history, tools and output share one window: Every token you add is a token you cannot generate.
Needle tests vs real long documents: A synthetic needle can pass while a messy PDF still fails.
Interview: what you put in the window: Standing rules, retrieved evidence, the user turn — and what you leave out.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.8: The Context Window (source)

nodes.title: M1.9 · LLM Capabilities & Failure Modes
nodes.summary: M1.9 in L1 · LLM 101, 7 topics: Common strengths; Common failure modes; Why hallucination happens.
checklist: Common strengths: Understand common strengths: summarization, text transformation, extraction, classification, semantic understanding, coding, translation, brainstorming, working with unstructured information, and few-shot adaptation.

Common failure modes: Understand common failure modes: hallucination, arithmetic mistakes, brittle reasoning, instruction-following failures, prompt sensitivity, context failures, outdated knowledge, nondeterminism, and confident incorrect answers.

Why hallucination happens: Understand hallucination mechanistically: an LLM is trained to generate a likely continuation, not to independently verify that every generated statement is true, which makes fluent incorrect answers possible.

Asking "how reliably?" instead of "can it?": Adopt the engineering question: instead of “Can GPT do this?”, ask “How reliably does this model perform this task under the conditions of my application?”
Hallucination as next-token confidence: Fluency is not a calibrated probability of truth.
Sycophancy and prompt-following: The model may agree with a wrong user claim.
Interview: how you bound a failure: Ground, validate, abstain, or route to a tool — do not 'prompt harder' only.

links.title: Level 1 module M1.9: LLM Capabilities & Failure Modes (source)

nodes.title: M1.10 · Understanding the Model Landscape
nodes.summary: M1.10 in L1 · LLM 101, 10 topics: Closed and API models; Open-weight models; Managed platforms & hosted open weights.
checklist: Closed and API models: Understand closed/API models through trade-offs involving frontier capability, convenience, infrastructure, privacy, vendor dependence, and control.
Open-weight models: Understand open-weight models through self-hosting, privacy, customization, infrastructure requirements, and operational complexity.

Managed platforms & hosted open weights: Understand the third path between them: managed platforms such as AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure AI Foundry serve both closed and open-weight models inside your own cloud account, and inference providers host open weights for you without any hardware of your own.
Other useful distinctions: Learn other useful distinctions: small vs large, dense vs Mixture-of-Experts, general-purpose vs specialized, reasoning vs non-reasoning, and text-only vs multimodal.
There is no universally best LLM: Internalize the core principle: there is no universally best LLM; the best model depends on the workload.
Knowledge cutoffs: Understand that a model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff, and that anything newer has to arrive through context, retrieval, or tools.

Versions, snapshots & deprecations: Track model versions and dated snapshots, and expect deprecations: the model behind a familiar name can change or be retired, so pin a version and re-test when it moves.
Open-weight licensing: Check the license before building on an open-weight model, since permissive, restricted-use, and non-commercial terms differ in what you are allowed to ship.
Deprecation and snapshot pins: Pin a dated snapshot in production; aliases move under you.
License vs weights vs API terms: Open weights can still forbid commercial use or training on outputs.

nodes.title: M1.11 · Benchmarks & Leaderboards
nodes.summary: M1.11 in L1 · LLM 101, 8 topics: What a benchmark is; Benchmarks quoted on model cards; Kinds of leaderboard.
checklist: What a benchmark is: Understand what a benchmark is: a fixed set of tasks with a fixed scoring method, used to measure different models against the same yardstick.

Benchmarks quoted on model cards: Recognize the benchmarks quoted on model cards — knowledge and reasoning tests such as MMLU and GPQA, coding tests, and mathematics tests — and know roughly what each one measures.
Kinds of leaderboard: Read the main kinds of leaderboard: human-preference rankings such as LMArena/Chatbot Arena, aggregated capability/cost/latency dashboards, and open-model leaderboards.

Why rank does not transfer: Understand why a leaderboard rank rarely transfers to your application: different prompts, different tasks, averaged scores, and someone else's definition of a good answer.
What inflates published scores: Understand the pitfalls that inflate published scores: data contamination, saturated benchmarks, overfitting to public test sets, and favorable run configurations.
From leaderboard to shortlist: Use benchmarks and leaderboards for the one thing they do well — narrowing a crowded field to a shortlist — and then judge the shortlist on your own examples.
Contamination and train-test overlap: A high score can mean the item leaked into training.
Your task is the only leaderboard that ships: Public ranks shortlist; your eval decides.

nodes.title: M1.12 · Choosing the Right Model
nodes.summary: M1.12 in L1 · LLM 101, 14 topics: Eight dimensions for model choice; Capability; Quality.
checklist: Eight dimensions for model choice: Evaluate models across eight dimensions:
Capability: Capability: Can it perform the task at all?
Quality: Quality: How reliably does it perform your specific task?
Latency: Latency: How quickly does it respond?
Cost: Cost: What will each request cost at your expected usage?
Context: Context: Can it accommodate the required input?
Modalities: Modalities: Do you need text, images, audio, or video?
Privacy & deployment: Privacy & deployment: Can you use an external API, do you need a managed platform inside your own cloud, or do you require self-hosting?
Product features: Product features: Do you require structured outputs, function calling, tools, streaming, or caching?
Reading model cards & pricing pages: Learn to critically read model cards, benchmark tables, pricing pages, context-window specifications, and API documentation.
Why benchmarks alone are not enough: Understand why benchmark scores alone should not determine model selection.

The selection workflow: Follow the workflow: Define task → Identify requirements → Shortlist models → Test on your own examples → Measure quality → Measure latency → Measure cost → Inspect failures → Choose the model.
A written decision log for model choice: Record the task, constraints, shortlist, and why you picked the winner.
Re-evaluating after a provider change: Re-run the golden set when the alias or price changes.

Why it matters on the job (10/10): This is the core of the daily work: calling models, getting structured output, tool use, retries, streaming, handling rate limits and timeouts. Almost every feature you build goes through it.

Goal of this level: Level 2 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: turn individual LLM calls into reliable software workflows — messages, streaming, structured outputs, tools, multi-step orchestration, concurrency, failure handling, and observability. RAG and agents come later.

nodes.title: M2.1 · First API calls & conversation state
nodes.summary: M2.1 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Messages, roles & usage metadata; APIs are stateless; Application state vs model context.
checklist: Messages, roles & usage metadata: Call OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs; work with models, messages, system instructions, user/assistant roles, response objects, stop reasons, and usage metadata.
APIs are stateless: Understand that most LLM APIs are fundamentally stateless and learn to maintain conversation history explicitly.
Application state vs model context: Distinguish application state from information currently present in the model's context.
Managing API keys safely: Manage API keys safely using environment variables, .env files, or secret managers; never expose server-side credentials in frontend code.
Inspecting the full response object: Inspect input/output tokens, request metadata, and model responses instead of treating the API as a simple prompt → string function.
Usage objects and billed tokens: Log prompt, completion and cache tokens on every call.
Idempotent client wrappers: Retries need a timeout and a request id, not a naked loop.
Interview: sketch the first production call: Key from env, timeout, log usage, never print the key.

nodes.title: M2.2 · Streaming
nodes.summary: M2.2 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 6 topics: Rendering output incrementally; TTFT & perceived latency; Accumulating and interrupting streams.
checklist: Rendering output incrementally: Stream model output incrementally and render partial responses in a terminal or UI.
TTFT & perceived latency: Understand TTFT, generation speed, perceived latency, and total latency.
Accumulating and interrupting streams: Accumulate streamed events into a complete response and handle cancellations, interrupted streams, network failures, and incomplete generations.
Backpressure when the UI is slow: Do not buffer an unbounded stream in memory.
Partial JSON during streaming: Do not parse an object until the stream completes or you use a streaming parser.
Interview: cancel a stream cleanly: Abort the HTTP body and stop billing as soon as the user hits stop.

nodes.title: M2.3 · LangChain fundamentals
nodes.summary: M2.3 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Why orchestration libraries exist; Models, templates & output parsers; Working across providers.
checklist: Why orchestration libraries exist: Understand why orchestration libraries exist and what LangChain abstracts over raw provider SDKs.
Models, templates & output parsers: Work with chat models, messages, prompt templates, output parsers, streaming, and model configuration.
Working across providers: Use LangChain with multiple model providers while understanding the underlying API calls it is making.
Composing pipelines with runnables: Learn the core composition model and build simple pipelines using prompts, models, parsers, and runnables.
Raw SDK vs LangChain: Compare equivalent implementations using raw SDKs and LangChain to understand convenience vs abstraction overhead.
LangChain is a layer, not the model: Keep the mental model that LangChain is an orchestration layer, not the LLM itself.
Vendor lock-in vs raw SDK: Frameworks hide providers; you still own retries, logging and schemas.
Debugging through a runnable: Print the rendered prompt and parsed output, not just the chain name.

nodes.title: M2.4 · Structured outputs
nodes.summary: M2.4 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Schema-constrained generation; Defining schemas; Provider-native vs framework support.
checklist: Schema-constrained generation: Generate schema-constrained outputs rather than relying on “please return JSON” prompting.
Defining schemas: Define schemas using JSON Schema/Pydantic; work with required fields, optional fields, enums, lists, nested objects, and typed responses.
Provider-native vs framework support: Implement structured outputs using both provider-native capabilities and LangChain abstractions.
Validating before use: Validate model outputs before passing them into application logic.
Syntactic validity vs semantic correctness: Distinguish syntactic validity from semantic correctness: valid JSON can still contain incorrect information.
Generate → validate → repair: Implement a generate → validate → accept / retry / repair / reject workflow for invalid outputs.
Enum and optional fields in schemas: Tight types beat a free-form string the parser cannot trust.
What to do when the model omits a field: Default in code or retry once with the validator error.

nodes.title: M2.5 · Function / tool calling
nodes.summary: M2.5 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 9 topics: Who chooses and who executes; Defining a tool; The full tool-calling loop.
checklist: Who chooses and who executes: Understand that the LLM normally chooses a tool and generates arguments; your application executes the actual function.
Defining a tool: Define tools using names, descriptions, parameter schemas, types, and required arguments.
The full tool-calling loop: Implement the full loop: user → LLM → tool request → execute tool → return result → LLM → final answer.
Tool-call IDs & returning results: Work with tool-call IDs and correctly insert tool results back into the conversation.
Provider APIs vs LangChain tools: Implement tool calling using provider APIs directly and understand how LangChain represents and executes tools.
Sequential, repeated & parallel calls: Handle sequential calls, multiple calls to the same tool, parallel calls, and workflows where one tool result determines the next tool call.
Tool failures & malformed arguments: Handle tool failures and malformed arguments instead of assuming every requested invocation is executable.
Tool choice auto vs required vs none: Force a tool when the turn must call it; none when it must not.
Interview: draw the tool loop: Model proposes, your code executes, you return a tool result, model finishes.

nodes.title: M2.6 · Designing good tools
nodes.summary: M2.6 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Names, descriptions & types; Ambiguous & overlapping tools; Too many undifferentiated tools.
checklist: Names, descriptions & types: Design tools with precise names, clear descriptions, minimal parameters, strong types, and useful error responses.
Ambiguous & overlapping tools: Understand how ambiguous or overlapping tools can cause incorrect tool selection.
Too many undifferentiated tools: Avoid giving the model huge numbers of poorly differentiated tools or unnecessary arguments.
Treating arguments as untrusted: Treat model-generated arguments as untrusted input: validate types, values, permissions, and potentially destructive operations before execution.
Tool descriptions are context: Understand that tool descriptions themselves are part of the context the model uses to decide what action to take.
One tool, one job: Split overlapping tools so the model is not guessing between twins.
Argument validation before side effects: Schema-valid is not business-valid; check ids and units in code.
Interview: rewrite a bad tool spec: Tighten the name, description and types until a stranger could implement it.

nodes.summary: M2.7 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Beyond prompt → model → answer; Sequential, routed & fan-out patterns; When to split a task.
checklist: Beyond prompt → model → answer: Move beyond prompt → model → answer and build workflows containing multiple LLM calls, tools, transformations, and application logic.
Sequential, routed & fan-out patterns: Implement common orchestration patterns: sequential pipelines, routing, conditional branches, and fan-out/fan-in.
When to split a task: Learn when to split a complex task into multiple specialized calls instead of using one enormous prompt.
Building by hand, then composing: Build some workflows manually to understand their control flow, then reproduce them using LangChain composition primitives.
Workflows vs agents: Understand the distinction between application-controlled workflows and the more autonomous agentic systems introduced later.
Routing tables vs an agent: A documented if/else over intent is easier to test than a free loop.
Fan-out then merge: Parallel calls need a join that handles one empty or failed branch.
Interview: when you refuse an agent: Stable, short workflows with a known graph stay as workflows.

nodes.title: M2.8 · Async, concurrency & batching
nodes.summary: M2.8 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: When concurrency helps; Running requests concurrently; Bounded concurrency & rate limits.
checklist: When concurrency helps: Understand synchronous vs asynchronous API calls and when concurrency improves throughput.
Running requests concurrently: Process many independent LLM requests concurrently rather than sequentially.
Bounded concurrency & rate limits: Use bounded concurrency so higher throughput does not immediately create rate-limit failures.
Async and batch execution: Apply async and batch execution using both provider SDKs and orchestration-layer abstractions.
The throughput / cost trade-off: Understand the trade-off between concurrency, throughput, latency, API limits, resource consumption, and cost.
Semaphore as the production primitive: Bound in-flight calls to the provider's rate, not to hope.
Batch APIs vs online: Overnight evals use batch; user-facing turns stay online with a timeout.
Interview: 1000 calls without getting banned: Concurrency cap, jittered backoff, and a budget alarm.

nodes.title: M2.9 · Robustness: retries, timeouts & fallbacks
nodes.summary: M2.9 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: Common API failures; What to retry and what to fail fast; Backoff, jitter, timeouts & degradation.
checklist: Common API failures: Recognize common API failures: authentication errors, invalid requests, rate limits, server errors, network failures, timeouts, context-limit errors, and malformed model outputs.

What to retry and what to fail fast: Decide which failures should be retried and which should fail immediately; for example, authentication errors generally should not be retried while transient server errors may be.
Backoff, jitter, timeouts & degradation: Implement exponential backoff, jitter, maximum retry counts, sensible request timeouts, and graceful degradation.
Model and provider fallbacks: Add model/provider fallbacks when appropriate, while understanding that fallback models may differ in quality and behavior.
Failures at the LLM and tool levels: Handle failures at both levels: LLM API failure and tool/API failure.
Where reliability logic belongs: Understand where reliability logic should live: provider SDK, orchestration layer, or your application code.
Retry maps for status codes: 429 and 503 retry; 400 and 401 do not.
Fallback that preserves the contract: A cheaper model must still emit the same schema.

nodes.summary: M2.10 in L2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration), 8 topics: What to record per request; Interactions as traces; Finding the failing step.
checklist: What to record per request: Track model, input tokens, output tokens, latency, retries, errors, tool calls, and estimated cost for every request.
Interactions as traces: Treat a multi-step LLM interaction as a trace rather than an isolated API call.
Finding the failing step: Inspect which step caused a failure, which call consumed the most tokens, which tool was selected, and where latency accumulated.
Tracing a full workflow: Use callbacks/tracing to understand LangChain workflows and connect individual model and tool calls into a single execution trace.
Logging you can actually debug with: Build enough logging and tracing that you can debug workflows without relying on scattered print() statements.
Trace ids across a multi-step call: One id from the user request through tools and the model.
Cost anomaly alerts: Page when tokens per request jump, not only when the process dies.
Interview: what you log and what you never log: Usage and ids yes; raw user PII and full prompts only if policy allows.

LlamaIndex: Explore LlamaIndex and how its abstractions and emphasis differ from LangChain.

A thin orchestrator you can replace: Keep provider calls behind a port so LangChain is not the domain.
End-to-end test of the streamed tool path: Fake the model, assert the tool ran and the UI got tokens.

nodes.title: Level 3 overview: Prompt Engineering
nodes.summary: Level 3 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: design instructions that make LLM behavior more reliable and predictable. Context engineering comes later.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (5/10): Interviewers rarely ask about it in depth; they assume you can do it. It doesn’t set you apart, and listing it on a resume as a headline skill can look junior.
Why it matters on the job (8/10): You write and revise prompts constantly. Small changes to instructions often fix problems faster than code changes, so it matters more on the job than in interviews.
Prerequisites: Level 2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration)
Goal of this level: Level 3 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: design instructions that make LLM behavior more reliable and predictable. Context engineering comes later.
Plan 8 modules and the capstone “Optimize a Real Prompt” before moving on

links.title: 100 Days of AI Engineering · Prompt Engineering

nodes.title: M3.1 · Anatomy of a prompt
nodes.summary: M3.1 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 9 topics: The parts of a prompt; Roles & instruction priority; Separating instructions from data; Prompt templates vs one-off prompts.
checklist: The parts of a prompt: Structure prompts using instructions, context, input, constraints, examples, and output requirements.
Roles & instruction priority: Use system/user/assistant roles correctly and understand instruction priority.
Separating instructions from data: Separate instructions clearly from user-provided or external data.
Prompt templates vs one-off prompts: Reuse a labelled template for production tasks instead of rewriting a blob each time.
Labelled sections and delimiters: Mark instructions, context, input and output spec with headings or XML-style tags.
Default order of prompt parts: Put stable rules first, examples next, and the changing input last so prefixes can cache.
Caching-friendly prompt layout: Keep a byte-stable prefix and isolate volatile user text at the end.
Common anatomy mistakes: Mixing the task into the data, burying the output spec, or leaving no rule for missing information.
Interview walkthrough of a support prompt: Be ready to sketch a ticket-classifier prompt by parts and justify the order.

links.title: Level 3 module M3.1: Anatomy of a prompt (source)

nodes.title: M3.2 · Zero-shot & few-shot prompting
nodes.summary: M3.2 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: When examples are needed; Designing few-shot examples; Example quality, diversity & order; Few-shot vs fine-tuning.
checklist: When examples are needed: Know when a clear zero-shot instruction is sufficient and when examples are needed.
Designing few-shot examples: Design useful few-shot examples that demonstrate desired behavior and output format.
Example quality, diversity & order: Understand how example quality, diversity, and ordering can affect results.
Few-shot vs fine-tuning: Distinguish few-shot prompting from fine-tuning.
Zero-shot failure patterns: Spot format drift, fuzzy label boundaries and style misses that examples should fix.
How many examples to use: Start with three to five targeted cases and stop when the test set stops improving.
Dynamic few-shot from a store: Retrieve similar labelled examples at request time instead of hard-coding a static set.
Label balance and recency bias: Mix classes and avoid clustering one label at the end of the prompt.
Cost of few-shot vs a clearer instruction: Measure tokens against a rewritten zero-shot before keeping examples.
Choosing zero-shot, few-shot or fine-tune: Pick the cheapest method that hits the measured quality bar.

links.title: Level 3 module M3.2: Zero-shot & few-shot prompting (source)

nodes.title: M3.3 · Reasoning & decomposition
nodes.summary: M3.3 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: When to prompt for reasoning; When reasoning is unnecessary; Decomposing complex tasks; Prompting reasoning models.
checklist: When to prompt for reasoning: Use reasoning-oriented prompting for complex logic, planning, mathematics, coding, and constraint-heavy tasks.
When reasoning is unnecessary: Know when extra reasoning is unnecessary for tasks such as extraction, classification, and rewriting.
Decomposing complex tasks: Break complex tasks into clearer subproblems or intermediate steps.
Prompting reasoning models: Adapt prompting for reasoning models rather than relying blindly on “think step by step.”
Chain-of-thought vs hidden reasoning: Know when visible steps help you debug and when a reasoning model should keep them internal.
Scratchpads and intermediate JSON: Ask for a short plan or fields before the final answer so you can check the work.
Plan-then-execute: Split planning from doing when a task has tools, multiple sources or irreversible actions.
When decomposition increases error: Avoid extra hops on simple extract-and-label work where each hop can drop a field.
Measuring reasoning quality: Score the final answer and the plan separately so fluent steps do not hide a wrong result.
Debugging a reasoning prompt: Drop forced step-by-step, add a schema, or switch model family when traces ramble.

nodes.title: M3.4 · System prompt design
nodes.summary: M3.4 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: What belongs in a system prompt; Stable rules vs task instructions; Handling missing or out-of-scope input; Lightweight behavioural guardrails.
checklist: What belongs in a system prompt: Define application purpose, behavior, constraints, boundaries, and output expectations in the system prompt.
Stable rules vs task instructions: Separate stable application rules from task-specific user instructions.
Handling missing or out-of-scope input: Specify what the model should do when information is missing, ambiguous, or outside scope.
Lightweight behavioural guardrails: Add lightweight behavioral guardrails without turning the system prompt into an enormous rulebook.
System prompt length and attention: Keep standing rules short; long policy dumps get ignored in the middle.
Persona vs policy: A voice is optional; permissions, refusals and output shape are not.
Tool and safety clauses: State which tools exist, what they must never do, and what requires confirmation.
Versioning the system prompt: Treat the system text as a versioned artefact and log the id with every call.
Conflicts with user and developer messages: Put durable rules in system, per-request facts in user, and never rely on priority as security.
Write a support-bot system prompt: In an interview, draft purpose, boundaries, missing-info rule and output shape in one screen.

links.title: Level 3 module M3.4: System prompt design (source)

nodes.title: M3.5 · Controlling output
nodes.summary: M3.5 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 11 topics: Controlling style, length & format; When prompting is not enough; Semantic instruction vs format enforcement; Style guides in the prompt.
checklist: Controlling style, length & format: Control response style, length, format, headings, labels, tables, and JSON through clear instructions and examples.
When prompting is not enough: Know when prompting is enough and when structured-output/schema enforcement from Level 2 is more reliable.
Semantic instruction vs format enforcement: Separate semantic instructions from programmatic format enforcement.
Style guides in the prompt: Encode tone, banned phrases and audience in a short reusable block.
Length budgets and stop conditions: Set max sentences or tokens and say what to cut first when the budget is tight.
JSON vs markdown vs tables: Choose a format for the consumer (code, human, or both) and show one example of it.
Repair loops after invalid output: Validate, send the error back once, then fail to a default rather than looping forever.
Provider structured-output APIs: Prefer schema-constrained decoding over hoping the model obeys a JSON please.
Refusal and empty-output handling: Define the exact object or label to return when the model must abstain.
Temperature vs format reliability: Lower temperature and use a schema when the parser is downstream.
Interview: enforce a schema: Walk through generate, validate, repair and the fallback your code owns.

nodes.title: M3.6 · Prompt reliability & debugging
nodes.summary: M3.6 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: Diagnosing prompt failures; Building a small test set; Comparing versions on the same examples; Reducing variance & regressions.
checklist: Diagnosing prompt failures: Diagnose failures caused by ambiguous instructions, conflicting constraints, poor examples, missing context, or unclear output requirements.
Building a small test set: Build a small test set containing normal cases, edge cases, and known failures.
Comparing versions on the same examples: Compare prompt versions on the same examples instead of judging them from individual responses.
Reducing variance & regressions: Reduce unnecessary output variance and regressions through systematic iteration.
Failure taxonomy for prompts: Tag misses as ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples or weak output spec.
Golden set design: Include easy, borderline, adversarial and regression cases with an expected shape.
Blind comparison and inter-rater: Hide which prompt produced the output when humans score quality.
Pinning model versions: Freeze the snapshot while you iterate the prompt so model drift is not confused with prompt drift.
Logging traces for debug: Store prompt id, model, input hash and raw output so a failure is replayable.
Interview: how you iterate a prompt: Describe measure, change one thing, re-run the same set, keep or revert.

nodes.title: M3.7 · Prompt versioning, cost & caching
nodes.summary: M3.7 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: Versioning prompts like code; Comparing on quality, latency & cost; Trimming unnecessary context; Prompt caching & reusable prefixes.
checklist: Versioning prompts like code: Version prompts like code and track which prompt/model combination produced each result.
Comparing on quality, latency & cost: Compare prompt variants using quality, latency, token usage, and cost.
Trimming unnecessary context: Remove unnecessary context and repeated instructions.
Prompt caching & reusable prefixes: Understand prompt caching and structure reusable prompt prefixes to benefit from caching where supported.
Prompt IDs in logs and traces: Stamp every request with prompt_version and model so cost and quality join in one query.
Token accounting: Split prefix, retrieved context and output tokens; cut the largest bucket first.
Cache breakpoints and prefix stability: Know where the provider caches and never put a timestamp or user id before that point.
A/B testing prompts in production: Split traffic, watch quality and cost together, and roll back on a quality drop.
Stale context and secret leakage in prefixes: Do not cache secrets or user-specific data in a shared prefix.
Interview: cut cost without losing quality: Cache the prefix, drop unused context, then consider a smaller model.

nodes.summary: M3.8 in Level 3 (Prompt Engineering), 10 topics: What prompt injection is; Recognising override attempts; Wording is not a security boundary; Deeper defences come later.
checklist: What prompt injection is: Understand prompt injection and why external/user-controlled text should be treated as untrusted data.
Recognising override attempts: Recognize attempts to override system instructions or extract hidden information.
Wording is not a security boundary: Understand that prompt wording alone is not a security boundary; permissions and sensitive actions must be controlled by application code.
Deeper defences come later: Leave deeper adversarial security and defenses for the later security level.
Direct vs indirect injection: A user can override you, and so can a retrieved page or a tool result.
Data exfiltration via prompts: Watch for requests that ask the model to dump system text, secrets or other users' data.
Isolation and privilege: Run the model with the least tools and the least data it needs for that turn.
Allow-lists for tools: Code decides which recipients, URLs and queries are legal; the model only proposes.
Human confirmation for side effects: Email, pay, delete and post wait for an explicit user or reviewer tick.
Interview: design a safe email-sender: Fence the draft, allow-list addresses, require confirm, log the action not the body.

nodes.title: M4.1 · Data ingestion & document processing
nodes.summary: M4.1 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Extracting from PDFs, HTML & DOCX; Cleaning while keeping structure; Duplicates, updates & re-indexing.
checklist: Extracting from PDFs, HTML & DOCX: Extract content from common sources such as PDFs, HTML, DOCX, and structured documents; understand when OCR is required.
Cleaning while keeping structure: Clean and normalize messy text while preserving useful document structure and metadata.
Duplicates, updates & re-indexing: Handle duplicate documents, document updates, and incremental re-indexing.
OCR vs born-digital text: Scanned PDFs need OCR and will drop tables; born-digital keeps structure.
Preserving headings and lists: Keep hierarchy in metadata so chunking can respect sections.
Incremental ingest and deletes: Re-index only changed documents and tombstone removals.
Interview: ingest a messy PDF corpus: Name extract, clean, dedupe, and how you would measure loss.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.1: Data ingestion & document processing (source)

nodes.title: M4.2 · Chunking strategies
nodes.summary: M4.2 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Why documents must be split; Fixed, recursive, structural & semantic; Size, overlap, boundaries & metadata.
checklist: Why documents must be split: Understand why documents must usually be split before embedding and retrieval.
Fixed, recursive, structural & semantic: Apply fixed-size, recursive, structural, and semantic chunking.
Size, overlap, boundaries & metadata: Reason about chunk size, overlap, boundaries, and metadata and how they affect retrieval quality.
Precise chunks vs context-rich chunks: Understand the trade-off between small precise chunks and larger context-rich chunks.
Parent-child and small-to-big: Retrieve a small chunk, send its parent for context.
Table and code block boundaries: Never split a table row or a function mid-chunk if you can avoid it.
Interview: pick a chunk size: Start from the embedding model's useful length, measure recall, then adjust overlap.

nodes.title: M4.3 · Embeddings fundamentals
nodes.summary: M4.3 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: What an embedding represents; Generating embeddings; Choosing an embedding model.
checklist: What an embedding represents: Understand embeddings as vector representations that capture semantic relationships between text.
Generating embeddings: Generate embeddings for documents and queries using an embedding model.
Choosing an embedding model: Understand dimensions, embedding model choice, multilingual/domain performance, cost, and latency trade-offs.
Vector spaces cannot be mixed: Understand that embeddings from different models/vector spaces generally cannot be mixed directly.
Instruction-tuned vs raw embedding models: Some embedders expect a query prefix; mismatch tanks recall.
Dimensionality and storage cost: Higher dims cost RAM and ANN quality is not automatic.
Interview: why you cannot mix spaces: Different embedders rotate the space; cosine across models is meaningless.

nodes.title: M4.4 · Similarity & semantic search
nodes.summary: M4.4 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Cosine, dot product & Euclidean; Semantic search from scratch; Semantic similarity vs keyword match.
checklist: Cosine, dot product & Euclidean: Understand cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance and how they are used to compare vectors.
Semantic search from scratch: Build a simple semantic-search system from scratch: query → embedding → similarity → top-k results.
Semantic similarity vs keyword match: Understand the difference between semantic similarity and exact keyword matching.
Where semantic search fails: Explore common failure cases such as exact names, IDs, numbers, and rare terminology.
Metric must match the index: Cosine vs L2 vs inner product is a training-and-index decision.
Keyword still wins on identifiers: SKUs, error codes and names often need BM25 alongside vectors.
Interview: when semantic search fails: Negation, exact ids, and recency — say what you add next.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.4: Similarity & semantic search (source)

nodes.title: M4.5 · Vector databases & ANN search
nodes.summary: M4.5 in L4 · RAG, 8 topics: Storing vectors in pgvector or Qdrant; Top-k search with metadata filters; Why ANN search exists.
checklist: Storing vectors in pgvector or Qdrant: Store embeddings, documents, IDs, and metadata in a vector database such as pgvector or Qdrant.
Top-k search with metadata filters: Perform top-k vector search with metadata filtering.
Why ANN search exists: Understand why brute-force search becomes expensive at scale and why Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search exists.
HNSW & IVF trade-offs: Build intuition for HNSW and IVF and their speed ↔ memory ↔ recall trade-offs without going deep into implementation mathematics.
Indexing, updates & deletes: Understand indexing, updates, deletes, and basic operational considerations.
Filters before or after ANN: Pre-filtering can empty a graph neighbourhood; know your engine's rule.
Recall vs latency knobs: ef/nprobe are product settings, not one-time defaults.
Interview: choose pgvector vs a dedicated store: Start in Postgres if the corpus is small; move when ANN ops dominate.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.5: Vector databases & ANN search (source)

nodes.title: M4.6 · Capstone: Build a Hybrid Search Engine
nodes.summary: M4.6 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Lexical retrieval & BM25; Sparse vs dense retrieval; Hybrid retrieval with RRF.
checklist: Lexical retrieval & BM25: Understand traditional lexical retrieval and BM25, and why keyword search can outperform embeddings for some queries.
Sparse vs dense retrieval: Compare sparse/BM25 retrieval with dense/vector retrieval.
Hybrid retrieval with RRF: Combine dense and sparse results using hybrid retrieval and techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
When hybrid retrieval helps: Understand when hybrid retrieval helps, especially for queries containing names, technical terms, IDs, numbers, and exact phrases.
RRF as the default merge: Reciprocal rank fusion needs no score calibration.
When hybrid does not help: If one channel already has high recall, the other only adds latency.
Interview: design hybrid search: Sparse + dense + RRF, then a reranker if the judge still misses.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.6: Capstone: Build a Hybrid Search Engine (source)

nodes.title: M4.8 · RAG architecture & when to use it
nodes.summary: M4.8 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: The core RAG pipeline; What RAG solves; When not to use RAG.
checklist: The core RAG pipeline: Understand the core pipeline: query → retrieve → assemble context → generate answer.
What RAG solves: Understand what RAG solves: private knowledge, frequently changing information, large knowledge bases, and source-grounded answers.
When not to use RAG: Know when not to use RAG: when the model already knows enough, the task is purely transformational, or the required knowledge can simply fit in context.
Retrieval failure vs generation failure: Distinguish retrieval failure from generation failure.
Fresh facts vs parametric memory: RAG is for changing or private knowledge, not for style.
Failure split: retrieve vs generate: Always measure both; a fluent wrong answer is often a miss at retrieval.
Interview: when you would not use RAG: Stable closed tasks, or when a database query is the real answer.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.8: RAG architecture & when to use it (source)

nodes.title: M4.9 · Baseline RAG from scratch
nodes.summary: M4.9 in L4 · RAG, 8 topics: Building the pipeline by hand; Retrieve, assemble, generate; Prompting for grounded answers.
checklist: Building the pipeline by hand: Build a complete RAG pipeline manually using the retrieval system built earlier in this level.
Retrieve, assemble, generate: Retrieve top-k chunks, assemble them into the prompt, and generate an answer grounded in the retrieved context.
Prompting for grounded answers: Design prompts that instruct the model to answer from supplied evidence and avoid unsupported claims.
Handling weak or missing context: Handle cases where retrieval returns weak, irrelevant, or insufficient context.
The effect of k and chunk ordering: Understand the effect of k, chunk ordering, and total context size on answer quality.
Citations as mandatory fields: Ask for quote-plus-id so you can check the span.
k, diversity and ordering: Adjacent near-duplicates waste the window; order by relevance, not ingest time.
Interview: ship a baseline RAG: Ingest, chunk, embed, top-k, grounded prompt, abstain rule, then evaluate.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.9: Baseline RAG from scratch (source)

nodes.title: M4.10 · Reranking
nodes.summary: M4.10 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Retrieve many, rerank, send the best; Cross-encoder & reranking models; Relevance gained, latency added.
checklist: Retrieve many, rerank, send the best: Understand the two-stage pattern: retrieve many candidates → rerank → send the best chunks to the LLM.
Cross-encoder & reranking models: Use cross-encoder or dedicated reranking models to reorder retrieved chunks.
Relevance gained, latency added: Understand why reranking can improve relevance while adding latency and cost.
When reranking adds little: Compare retrieval with and without reranking and understand when reranking provides little benefit.
Cross-encoder cost model: Rerank a shortlist, never the whole corpus.
When the first-stage already ranks well: Skip the reranker until an eval proves the lift.
Interview: place a reranker: Retrieve 50, rerank 8, send 4 — and measure extra latency.

nodes.title: M4.11 · Query transformation & RAG-Fusion
nodes.summary: M4.11 in L4 · RAG, 8 topics: Why the user question is a poor query; Rewriting, expansion, multi-query & HyDE; RAG-Fusion.
checklist: Why the user question is a poor query: Understand why the user's original question is not always the best retrieval query.
Rewriting, expansion, multi-query & HyDE: Apply query rewriting, query expansion, multi-query retrieval, and HyDE.
RAG-Fusion: Understand RAG-Fusion: generate multiple queries, retrieve for each, and combine rankings using techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Handling ambiguous questions: Use multiple retrieval queries for ambiguous, multi-faceted, or poorly phrased questions.
The extra calls it costs: Understand the trade-off between improved retrieval and additional LLM calls, latency, and cost.
When to skip transformation: Avoid query transformation when baseline retrieval already performs well.
HyDE failure on precise queries: Hypothetical documents can drift off an identifier-heavy question.
Budget for extra rewrite calls: Each transform is another model call; skip on easy lookups.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.11: Query transformation & RAG-Fusion (source)

nodes.title: M4.12 · Grounding, citations & abstention
nodes.summary: M4.12 in L4 · RAG, 8 topics: Answering from evidence; Attaching claims to sources; Citations are not grounding.
checklist: Answering from evidence: Generate answers grounded in retrieved evidence rather than unsupported model knowledge.
Attaching claims to sources: Attach claims to their supporting documents/chunks and produce useful source citations.
Citations are not grounding: Understand that having citations is not the same as being grounded; the cited source must actually support the claim.
Abstaining on insufficient evidence: Detect insufficient evidence and respond with an appropriate “I don't know / insufficient information” instead of forcing an answer.
Keeping evidence and synthesis distinct: Keep retrieved evidence and model-generated synthesis clearly distinguishable.
Quote-then-answer vs answer-then-cite: Generating first invites invented sources.
Abstain object in the schema: A required 'insufficient_evidence' path beats a hedged paragraph.
Interview: show a grounded answer: Point at the span, refuse if missing, and never cite a title you did not retrieve.

links.title: Level 4 module M4.12: Grounding, citations & abstention (source)

nodes.title: M4.13 · RAG variants & advanced patterns
nodes.summary: M4.13 in L4 · RAG, 11 topics: Naive → Advanced → adaptive RAG; Self-RAG; CRAG (Corrective RAG).
checklist: Naive → Advanced → adaptive RAG: Understand the progression from Naive RAG → Advanced RAG → adaptive/self-correcting RAG architectures.
Self-RAG: Learn Self-RAG: retrieval is performed when needed and the model reflects on retrieved evidence and its generated response.
CRAG (Corrective RAG): Learn CRAG (Corrective RAG): evaluate retrieved evidence and trigger corrective retrieval when the initial results are weak.
Adaptive RAG: Learn Adaptive RAG: dynamically decide whether retrieval is required and which retrieval strategy should be used.
Iterative RAG: Understand iterative RAG, where retrieval and generation repeat until enough evidence has been gathered.
Multi-hop RAG: Understand multi-hop RAG, where answering requires several retrieval steps or combining evidence from multiple sources.
Graph RAG: Learn Graph RAG: represent entities and relationships as a graph and retrieve/summarize information using graph structure rather than relying purely on vector similarity.
When Graph RAG is useful: Build intuition for when Graph RAG is useful: highly connected knowledge, entity relationships, global questions, and information spread across many documents.
Choosing by failure mode, not novelty: Compare advanced approaches on quality, complexity, latency, cost, and failure mode addressed rather than assuming more advanced RAG is always better.
Pick the variant from the failure: Multi-hop for chained facts; corrective RAG for bad first retrieval.
Graph RAG ops cost: Entity graphs need maintenance; do not start there.

nodes.summary: M4.14 in L4 · RAG, 7 topics: Rebuilding with LlamaIndex or LangChain; Indexes, retrievers & query engines; Framework reranking & query transforms.
checklist: Rebuilding with LlamaIndex or LangChain: Rebuild the manually created RAG pipeline using LlamaIndex or LangChain.
Indexes, retrievers & query engines: Work with framework abstractions for ingestion, indexes, retrievers, rerankers, query engines, and citations.
Framework reranking & query transforms: Implement common RAG improvements such as reranking and query transformation using framework components.
Framework vs hand-built: Compare the framework implementation with the hand-built version on control, development speed, debugging, and complexity.
Frameworks hide the prompt: Log the final assembled context before you trust the abstraction.
Parity test vs the hand-built baseline: A framework must not lose the abstain or citation rule.
Interview: defend a framework choice: Speed of iteration, then show you can still inspect retrieve and generate.

nodes.title: M5.1 · What is an agent?
nodes.summary: M5.1 in L5 · AI Agents, 8 topics: The agent loop; Call vs chain vs workflow vs agent; Where agents are useful.
checklist: The agent loop: Understand the basic loop: goal → decide → act → observe → repeat → finish.
Call vs chain vs workflow vs agent: Distinguish LLM call vs chain vs workflow vs agent, especially based on who decides what happens next.
Where agents are useful: Understand where agents are useful: open-ended, multi-step tasks where the execution path cannot be fully predetermined.
When a workflow is better: Know when a deterministic workflow is simpler, cheaper, and more reliable.
The components of an agent: Understand the basic components of an agent: model, instructions, tools, state/memory, control loop, stopping conditions.
State, tools, policy and the loop: Name the four pieces before drawing boxes.
Interview: agent vs workflow: Use an agent when the next step is unknown; a workflow when the graph is known.
The user-visible contract: Progress, cancel, and a final artefact — not a hidden chain of thought.
