nodes.title: M5.2 · ReAct, planning & reflection
nodes.summary: M5.2 in L5 · AI Agents, 9 topics: The ReAct pattern; Writing the loop by hand first; Step-by-step vs plan-first.
checklist: The ReAct pattern: Understand the ReAct pattern: the agent alternates between deciding what to do and acting on the environment.
Writing the loop by hand first: Implement a simple agent loop manually before using a framework.
Step-by-step vs plan-first: Understand step-by-step execution vs plan-first execution.
Decomposing and revising plans: Break complex goals into subtasks and dynamically revise plans as new information appears.
Reflection & self-correction: Use reflection/self-correction when actions fail or results are insufficient.
Stopping conditions & loop protection: Implement stopping conditions, maximum steps, and protection against repetitive loops.
What planning costs: Understand that more planning/reflection can increase quality but also latency and cost.
Reflection that actually checks work: A second pass needs a rubric or a test, not 'think harder'.
Hard stop conditions: Max steps, max cost, and a user cancel beat a hopeful loop.

links.title: Level 5 module M5.2: ReAct, planning & reflection (source)

nodes.title: M5.3 · Tools for agents
nodes.summary: M5.3 in L5 · AI Agents, 9 topics: From tool calling to agentic tool use; Designing tools for agents; Improving selection & arguments.
checklist: From tool calling to agentic tool use: Extend Level 2 tool calling into agentic tool use where the model repeatedly selects among available capabilities.
Designing tools for agents: Design tools with clear names, descriptions, schemas, typed arguments, useful outputs, and useful error messages.
Improving selection & arguments: Improve tool selection and argument correctness.
Sequential, parallel & repeated calls: Handle sequential, dependent, parallel, and repeated tool calls.
Recovering from tool failures: Handle tool failures and allow the agent to recover or choose an alternative.
Limiting tool-result size: Limit the size of tool results returned to the model so context does not become overwhelmed.
Read-only vs consequential tools: Separate read-only tools from consequential tools and add confirmation/permission checks where necessary.
Consequential tools need a confirm: Email, pay, delete wait for an explicit tick.
Truncating tool results: Return a summary plus a store id; do not dump 20k tokens into the window.

links.title: Level 5 module M5.3: Tools for agents (source)

nodes.title: M5.4 · MCP (Model Context Protocol)
nodes.summary: M5.4 in L5 · AI Agents, 9 topics: Why MCP exists; Host → client → server; Tool calling vs MCP.
checklist: Why MCP exists: Understand why MCP exists: provide a standardized way for AI applications to connect to external tools, resources, and prompts.
Host → client → server: Understand the host → client → server architecture and the responsibility of each component.

Tool calling vs MCP: Distinguish ordinary function calling from MCP: tool calling describes how a model requests an action, while MCP standardizes how external capabilities are exposed to AI applications.
Building an MCP server: Build an MCP server that exposes tools/resources from a real system such as a database, filesystem, SaaS application, or internal API.
Schemas, transports & auth: Work with schemas, capabilities, errors, local/remote transports, and authentication.
Building and connecting a client: Build/use an MCP client and connect it to one or more servers.
Permissions & untrusted servers: Understand permissions, trust boundaries, and the risk of connecting to untrusted MCP servers.
Untrusted MCP servers: Treat third-party tools as hostile; scope tokens and review schemas.
Transport and auth choices: Stdio for local; HTTP plus auth for anything remote.

links.title: Level 5 module M5.4: MCP (Model Context Protocol) (source)

nodes.title: M5.5 · Memory basics
nodes.summary: M5.5 in L5 · AI Agents, 10 topics: History, state, short- & long-term memory; Short-term memory; Long-term memory.
checklist: History, state, short- & long-term memory: Distinguish conversation history, state, short-term memory, and long-term memory.
Short-term memory: Implement short-term memory so an agent can retain information during a conversation or task.
Long-term memory: Implement basic long-term memory using persistent stores or retrieval-backed memory.
Storing what is worth keeping: Store useful facts, preferences, summaries, or previous outcomes instead of blindly preserving every message.
Retrieving only relevant memories: Retrieve relevant memories when needed rather than injecting the entire history into every request.
Write → retrieve → update → forget: Understand basic memory operations: write → retrieve → update → forget.
Trimming & summarizing growth: Handle growing conversations through trimming or summarization.
Offloading comes later: Keep deeper context offloading/compression strategies for the later Context Engineering level.
What is worth remembering: Decisions, user prefs, and open tasks — not every chat line.
Forgetting as a feature: TTL and explicit delete keep memory from rotting.

nodes.title: M5.6 · Multi-agent architectures
nodes.summary: M5.6 in L5 · AI Agents, 14 topics: Why more than one agent; Common patterns; Orchestrator → workers.
checklist: Why more than one agent: Understand why multiple agents may help when tasks require different tools, instructions, models, permissions, or areas of expertise.
Common patterns: Learn common patterns:
Orchestrator → workers: orchestrator → workers
Sequential handoffs: sequential handoffs
Parallel specialists: parallel specialists
Hierarchical supervisor/worker: hierarchical supervisor/worker architectures.
Building an orchestrator: Build an orchestrator that decomposes work and delegates tasks to specialist agents.
Passing state & aggregating output: Pass useful state/context between agents and aggregate their outputs.
Worker failure & escalation: Handle worker failures, retries, reassignment, and escalation.
What goes wrong with many agents: Understand common multi-agent problems: duplicated work, coordination overhead, context growth, conflicting results, latency, and cost.
A2A vs MCP: Understand A2A as an interoperability approach for independently built agents and contrast it conceptually with MCP: MCP connects agents to tools/resources; A2A connects agents to agents.
When one strong agent is better: Learn when multiple agents genuinely improve specialization and when one strong agent with several tools is preferable.
Handoff contracts: Workers return a typed result or a typed failure, never a vibe.
When one agent is enough: Extra agents add coordination bugs faster than they add quality.

nodes.title: M5.7 · Building agents with LangGraph
nodes.summary: M5.7 in L5 · AI Agents, 12 topics: What LangGraph is for; State, nodes & edges; Building nodes.
checklist: What LangGraph is for: LangGraph is positioned as a low-level orchestration framework/runtime for long-running, stateful agents.
State, nodes & edges: Model agent execution using state, nodes, and edges.
Building nodes: Build nodes for model calls, tools, processing logic, and decisions.
Conditional edges: Use conditional edges to dynamically determine the next action.
Loops for retries & iteration: Implement loops for repeated tool use, retries, and iterative execution.
Checkpointing & persistence: Add checkpointing/persistence so execution can survive interruptions.
Resuming long runs: Resume long-running agent runs rather than restarting them from scratch.
Human-in-the-loop interrupts: Add human-in-the-loop interrupts for actions requiring approval or intervention.
Inspecting state to debug: Inspect agent state to debug why a particular execution path was taken.
When a graph beats a loop: Understand when graph-based orchestration offers more control than a simple agent loop.
Checkpoints you can resume: Persist state after each node so a crash is not a restart.
Human interrupt as a first-class edge: Approval is a node, not a comment in the prompt.

Persisting state to resume: Persist enough execution state to resume after interruption.
Fallbacks & human escalation: Add fallback actions and human escalation when the agent cannot continue safely.
Surfacing progress to users: Surface useful progress to users: current task, tool/action being performed, results, sources, and requests for approval.
Cancel, pause, resume, redirect: Allow users to cancel, pause, resume, or redirect long-running work.
Understandable without exposing reasoning: Avoid exposing unnecessary private reasoning while still making execution understandable.
Surfacing progress without leaking chain-of-thought: Show steps as user-safe titles.
Idempotent writes: A retried 'create ticket' must not open two tickets.

nodes.title: Level 6 overview: Context Engineering
nodes.summary: Level 6 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: manage the model’s limited context window deliberately — decide what enters, what stays, what gets compressed, and what gets moved outside — and build the agent harness that applies these decisions across long-running work.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (6/10): Rarely asked as a topic by name. It mostly helps you give better answers in RAG and agent questions, which can set you apart in senior-level discussions.

Why it matters on the job (8/10): Once systems grow, quality depends heavily on what goes into the model’s input. It’s often the hidden cause of a system getting worse over time or becoming expensive.
Prerequisites: Level 5 · AI Agents

Goal of this level: Level 6 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: manage the model’s limited context window deliberately — decide what enters, what stays, what gets compressed, and what gets moved outside — and build the agent harness that applies these decisions across long-running work.
Plan 8 modules and the capstone “Context-Managed Long-Horizon Agent” before moving on

nodes.title: M6.1 · The context window as a resource
nodes.summary: M6.1 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Context as a budget; Context rot & lost-in-the-middle; Inspecting what actually enters.
checklist: Context as a budget: Treat context as a limited budget rather than “more is always better.”
Context rot & lost-in-the-middle: Understand context rot, distraction, conflicting context, lost-in-the-middle, and token/cost growth.
Inspecting what actually enters: Inspect what actually enters the model’s window and identify which parts are useful versus noise.
Allocating the budget: Allocate rough budgets across instructions, conversation history, retrieval, memory, tools, and working state.
Budget inspection: Log per-request token counts by section so you can see which bucket is eating the window.
Token accounting: Split system, history, retrieval, tools and output tokens; cut the largest bucket first.
Per-turn budget report: Emit a one-line breakdown after each model call and keep it in traces, not only logs.
Overflow policy: Decide what happens when a turn exceeds the budget: refuse, compress, or drop the oldest history.
Defending a window size: Be ready to say why you chose 8k versus 128k for a given product and what you measured.

links.title: Level 6 module M6.1: The context window as a resource (source)

nodes.title: M6.2 · Context selection & assembly
nodes.summary: M6.2 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Assembling the window deliberately; Always present, retrieved, or excluded; Prioritising what matters.
checklist: Assembling the window deliberately: Assemble instructions + conversation history + retrieved knowledge + memory + tool definitions/results + application state deliberately.
Always present, retrieved, or excluded: Decide what should be always present, dynamically retrieved, summarized, or excluded.
Prioritising what matters: Prioritize information based on relevance, importance, recency, and reliability.
Ordering so sources stay distinguishable: Order and structure context so instructions, evidence, memory, and user data remain clearly distinguishable.
Cutting redundant & stale context: Avoid redundant, stale, contradictory, or irrelevant context.
Source tags on every block: Prefix each injected span with a stable source label so the model and your logs can cite it.
Assembly order tests: Swap block order and check whether answers still cite the right evidence.
Recency versus reliability: Write a rule for when a newer message beats a more trusted document.
Conflict resolution before the call: Drop or flag contradictory snippets instead of stuffing both into the same window.

links.title: Level 6 module M6.2: Context selection & assembly (source)

nodes.title: M6.3 · Compression & compaction
nodes.summary: M6.3 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Summarizing history without losing goals; Compacting large tool outputs; Rolling & hierarchical summaries.
checklist: Summarizing history without losing goals: Summarize growing conversation history while preserving goals, constraints, decisions, and unresolved work.
Compacting large tool outputs: Compact large tool outputs before feeding them back into the model.
Rolling & hierarchical summaries: Apply rolling summaries and hierarchical summarization for long-running tasks.
Preserving exact structured data: Preserve exact structured information separately when summarization could lose important details.
Reduction vs information loss: Understand the trade-off between context reduction and information loss.
Compaction quality checks: Diff a compacted history against a gold list of goals, IDs and open questions.
Loss budget for summaries: Cap how many named entities and numbers a summary may drop before you refuse to compact.
Two-tier notes: Keep a short rolling summary for the model and a longer external note you can rehydrate.
When not to summarize: Leave short, high-stakes turns such as approvals, prices and IDs verbatim.

nodes.title: M6.4 · Memory & state offloading
nodes.summary: M6.4 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Scratchpads, files & external stores; Active context vs stored context; Persisting plans & progress.
checklist: Scratchpads, files & external stores: Move information outside the active window using scratchpads, files, databases, memory stores, task state, and working notes.
Active context vs stored context: Distinguish active context from information that can be stored externally and retrieved later.
Persisting plans & progress: Persist plans, completed steps, decisions, intermediate results, and important facts across long-running tasks.
Note-taking agents: Build note-taking agents that write useful information externally and recall it when required.
Remembering vs freeing space: Understand the distinction between memory for remembering and offloading for freeing context space.
Tool-result stores: Write large tool payloads to an id-keyed store and put only a pointer plus a short digest in the window.
Retrieval keys for offloaded state: Index offloaded notes by task, entity and recency so a later turn can fetch them.
Stale-memory eviction: Expire or rewrite notes that a later decision has superseded.
Pointer-not-payload rule: Never paste a file back into context when a path plus a one-line claim will do.

links.title: Level 6 module M6.4: Memory & state offloading (source)

nodes.title: M6.5 · Long-context strategies
nodes.summary: M6.5 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Why big windows do not solve it; Managing lost-in-the-middle; Stuffing vs retrieval vs summarization.
checklist: Why big windows do not solve it: Understand why large context windows do not eliminate context-engineering problems.
Managing lost-in-the-middle: Manage lost-in-the-middle using better positioning, selective retrieval, and context restructuring.
Stuffing vs retrieval vs summarization: Compare full-context stuffing, retrieval-over-history, summarization, hierarchical context, and selective loading.
More context or better context: Decide when to give the model more context versus retrieve only the relevant parts.
Lost-in-the-middle tests: Place a known fact at the start, middle and end of a long prompt and measure recall.
Needle placement sweeps: Move a single required constraint through the window and record where answers break.
Position-aware packing: Put instructions and the current question at the edges; bury low-value history in the middle.
Long-context eval set: Keep a fixture of long traces with labelled needles for regression tests.
When a bigger window is worth it: Use a long window only when retrieval cannot reconstruct the needed span.

nodes.title: M6.6 · Tool context management
nodes.summary: M6.6 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: Tool definitions compete for space; Exposing only relevant tools; Filtering large tool outputs.
checklist: Tool definitions compete for space: Understand that tool definitions and tool results also compete for context-window space.
Exposing only relevant tools: Dynamically expose only the tools relevant to the current task where possible.
Filtering large tool outputs: Summarize or filter large API/search/database outputs before returning them to the model.
Keeping full results externally: Keep full tool results externally and retrieve details again when required.
Stopping observation build-up: Prevent long agent loops from accumulating unnecessary observations and tool output.
Tool schema budgets: Count tokens in each tool JSON schema and drop unused fields before the call.
Result store plus digest: Persist the full tool result and return an id, a row count and a short excerpt.
Tool-loop observation caps: Cap how many raw observations stay in the window across a multi-step loop.
Dynamic tool menus: Swap the tool list when the task phase changes instead of shipping every schema every turn.

links.title: Level 6 module M6.6: Tool context management (source)

nodes.title: M6.7 · Context caching & efficiency
nodes.summary: M6.7 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 9 topics: The cost of resending static context; Structuring for cache hits; Stable context vs changing state.
checklist: The cost of resending static context: Understand how repeatedly sending large static contexts affects cost and latency.
Structuring for cache hits: Structure stable instructions and reusable context to benefit from prompt/context caching where supported.
Stable context vs changing state: Separate stable context from rapidly changing task state.
Cutting redundant tokens: Reduce redundant tokens while preserving useful information.
Measuring cache utilization: Measure token usage, cache utilization, latency, and cost rather than optimizing blindly.
Cache breakpoints: Know where the provider hashes the prefix and never put a timestamp, user id or random nonce before that point.
Prefix stability checks: Hash the cached prefix in CI so a one-line prompt edit does not silently bust the cache.
Cache hit rate in traces: Record cache-read versus cache-write tokens on every request and alert when the hit rate drops.
What not to cache: Keep secrets, per-user personal data and one-off tool results out of the stable prefix.

nodes.title: M6.8 · Capstone: Context-Managed Long-Horizon Agent
nodes.summary: M6.8 in Level 6 (Context Engineering), 12 topics: What an agent harness is; Harness problems vs model problems; Designing the agent loop.
checklist: [The agent harness] What an agent harness is: Understand the harness as everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, system prompt, tool set, context management, state, permissions, and the environment it acts in.

[The agent harness] Harness problems vs model problems: Recognize that the same model can succeed or fail on the same task depending on its harness, and that many agent failures are harness problems rather than model problems.

[The agent harness] Designing the agent loop: Design the agent loop: how model calls and tool calls alternate, how results and errors are fed back, and when to stop using step, time, and token limits.

[The agent harness] What the harness enforces: Decide what the harness enforces versus what the model decides: fixed workflow steps, permission checks, human approval for risky actions, and safe defaults.

[Harnesses for long-running work] Work across many context windows: Structure work that spans many context windows: an initial run that sets up the environment, plan, and task list, and later runs that read progress notes, complete one task at a time, and record what changed.

[Harnesses for long-running work] Durable artifacts as the source of truth: Use durable artifacts as the source of truth between runs, such as progress files, task lists, git commits, and tests, rather than conversation history.

[Harnesses for long-running work] Self-run feedback loops: Give the agent feedback loops it can run itself, such as tests, linters, type checks, and end-to-end checks, so it verifies work before marking it done.

[Harnesses for long-running work] An environment agents can read: Make the environment legible to the agent: short instruction files (such as AGENTS.md), a clear project structure, and documentation written to be read by agents.
[Harnesses for long-running work] Sub-agents for isolated context: Use sub-agents to give focused subtasks a fresh, isolated context and return only condensed results.
Context budget in the harness: Give the harness an explicit token budget and a policy for compact, offload or stop.
Progress file as the window: Treat the progress file as what survives a window reset, not the chat transcript.
Isolated sub-agent contracts: Specify what a sub-agent may see and what it must return so the parent window stays small.

Managed vs keep-everything comparison: Compare the context-managed version against a naive “keep everything” implementation on coherence, token usage, latency, and cost.

nodes.title: Level 7 overview: LLM Evaluations
nodes.summary: Level 7 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Design, execute, and automate comprehensive evaluations for Large Language Models and AI applications to ensure quality, safety, and reliability in production environments.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (8/10): Increasingly a decisive question: “How would you know your system works?” Most candidates answer weakly, so a concrete answer (test sets, LLM-as-judge, metrics) sets you apart sharply.
Why it matters on the job (10/10): Without evals, every change is a guess. Teams that measure ship faster and with more confidence, and this is where much of the senior-level work happens.
Prerequisites: Level 4 · RAG  Level 5 · AI Agents

Goal of this level: Level 7 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Design, execute, and automate comprehensive evaluations for Large Language Models and AI applications to ensure quality, safety, and reliability in production environments.
Plan 9 modules before moving on

nodes.summary: M7.1 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 8 topics: Pitfalls of vibe testing; Deterministic vs probabilistic testing; Model evals vs application evals.
checklist: Pitfalls of vibe testing: Understand the pitfalls of “vibe testing” by examining real-world failure case studies like Air Canada.
Deterministic vs probabilistic testing: Navigate the differences between deterministic software testing and probabilistic LLM systems.
Model evals vs application evals: Distinguish between evaluating core foundation model capabilities and testing complete application workflows.
The end-to-end evaluation workflow: Implement an end-to-end evaluation process covering task definition, criteria, datasets, execution, analysis, and iteration.
Unit, slice and end-to-end evals: Test retrieval, generation and the product separately.
Vibe testing as a prototype only: Pair it with a frozen set the moment a second person uses the app.
Interview: your first eval: 30 cases, expected shape, one judge or checker, run on every prompt change.
Who owns the golden set: Product plus engineering; it is a living artefact, not a data-science side quest.

checklist: Programmatic, human & LLM-as-a-Judge: Categorize evaluation execution mechanisms into Programmatic, Human, and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches.
Reference-based vs reference-free: Understand reference-based vs reference-free evaluation.
When a Golden Dataset is required: Determine when a Golden Dataset answer key is required versus when evaluation can rely entirely on LLM judgment.
Matching method to behaviour: Choose the appropriate evaluation method based on whether the target behavior is deterministic, semantic, subjective, or operational.
LLM-as-judge calibration: Spot-check the judge against humans before you trust the score.
Exact-match vs rubric: Use code for format; use a rubric for quality.
Interview: pick a method: Programmatic first, human for new failure types, judge for scale.

nodes.title: M7.3 · Offline vs online evaluations
nodes.summary: M7.3 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 8 topics: Offline suites for pre-release testing; Post-deployment production risks; System metrics vs quality metrics.
checklist: Offline suites for pre-release testing: Use offline evaluation suites for pre-release testing, version comparison, experimentation, and preventing performance regression.
Post-deployment production risks: Identify post-deployment production risks including unexpected inputs, emergent systematic failures, changing user behavior, and data drift.
System metrics vs quality metrics: Differentiate automatically captured system metrics such as latency, token usage, and errors from LLM-computed quality metrics such as hallucination or relevance.
Continuous online evaluation pipeline: Implement a continuous online evaluation pipeline through production logging, sampling, dashboarding, and alerting.
Feeding failures back offline: Feed important production failures back into the offline evaluation dataset.
Online shadow traffic: Score production inputs without changing the user reply.
Feedback that becomes a case: A thumbs-down with the retrieved context is tomorrow's offline item.
Interview: offline vs online: Offline gates a release; online tells you the mix shifted.

nodes.title: M7.4 · Model evaluations & benchmarking
nodes.summary: M7.4 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 7 topics: Core LLM capabilities; Anatomy of a benchmark; Public leaderboards.
checklist: Core LLM capabilities: Explore core LLM capabilities such as knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, coding, instruction following, long-context understanding, multimodal capability, safety, and tool use.
Anatomy of a benchmark: Analyze the anatomy of a benchmark through its dataset, prompts, run configuration, scoring method, and result aggregation.
Public leaderboards: Understand how public leaderboards compare foundation models.
Benchmark pitfalls: Identify benchmark pitfalls including data contamination, score saturation, benchmark overfitting, and configuration gaming.
Task transfer is the real test: A leaderboard win that fails your tickets is not a win.
Reading a model card like a sceptic: Training data, cutoff, safety, and the eval they chose to show.
Interview: why you ignored a rank: Contamination, wrong task, or a cost you cannot pay.

nodes.title: M7.5 · The evolution of knowledge benchmarks
nodes.summary: M7.5 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 6 topics: From MMLU to harder knowledge tests; Human exams as benchmarks; GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, HLE.
checklist: From MMLU to harder knowledge tests: Trace the progression from benchmarks such as MMLU and TruthfulQA toward harder tests of knowledge and factual reliability.
Human exams as benchmarks: Understand the use of human exams in benchmarks such as AGIEval to compare human and model capabilities.
GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, HLE: Explore harder benchmarks such as GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, and Humanity's Last Exam.
Why benchmarks keep getting harder: Understand why benchmarks continually become harder as frontier models saturate older datasets.
Saturation means you need a harder set: When everyone scores 90, the benchmark stopped discriminating.
Human exams vs product tasks: GPQA is a filter, not a substitute for your tickets.

nodes.title: M7.6 · Custom model evaluations
nodes.summary: M7.6 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 8 topics: Evaluating on your actual task; Shortlisting candidate models; Building a custom eval dataset.
checklist: Evaluating on your actual task: Move beyond public benchmarks and evaluate models on the actual task your application needs to solve.
Shortlisting candidate models: Use leaderboards and aggregation platforms to shortlist candidate models based on capability, latency, context, and cost.
Building a custom eval dataset: Build a custom evaluation dataset for a real task such as Text-to-SQL.
Like-for-like model comparison: Compare shortlisted models using the same inputs, prompts, parameters, and scoring criteria.
Estimating usage & token cost: Estimate API usage and token costs and use techniques such as prompt caching where appropriate.
Quality / latency / cost trade-off: Select the model that offers the best task-specific quality / latency / cost trade-off, rather than simply choosing the highest-ranked general model.
Stratify the custom set: Easy, hard, adversarial, and the last five production misses.
Cost model beside the quality table: Tokens and latency are columns, not footnotes.

nodes.title: M7.7 · Building an eval suite & regression testing
nodes.summary: M7.7 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 8 topics: Component, pipeline & application levels; Versioning tests, configs & results; Experiment tracking & baselines.
checklist: Component, pipeline & application levels: Structure evaluations across component level, pipeline level, and application level depending on what is being tested.
Versioning tests, configs & results: Maintain versioned test cases, evaluation configurations, prompts, models, and results.
Experiment tracking & baselines: Track experiments and compare new versions against established baselines.
CI/CD quality gates: Build automated CI/CD quality gates so changes cannot ship when important metrics regress.
Self-improving golden dataset: Create a self-improving loop by adding edge cases and failures discovered in production back into the offline golden dataset.
Quality alongside latency & cost: Track quality together with latency and cost so improvements in one area do not silently damage another.
A quality gate in CI: Fail the build on a statistically meaningful drop, not on one flaky case.
Baseline you can roll back to: Keep the last shipped prompt and score next to the candidate.

nodes.title: M7.8 · RAG Evals
nodes.summary: M7.8 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 28 topics: Four levels of RAG evaluation; Evaluating the retriever alone; Diagnosing missed & noisy retrieval.
checklist: Four levels of RAG evaluation: Evaluate a RAG system at component, pipeline, application, and safety levels, rather than treating it as one black-box system.
[Component-level evaluation] Evaluating the retriever alone: Evaluate the retriever independently to determine whether it finds the information required to answer the question.
[Component-level evaluation] Diagnosing missed & noisy retrieval: Diagnose cases where the retriever completely misses the relevant context or retrieves excessive irrelevant/noisy chunks.

[Component-level evaluation] Retrieval metrics: Measure retrieval effectiveness using metrics such as Contextual Recall, Contextual Precision, Recall@k, and other ranking-aware metrics where appropriate.

[Component-level evaluation] Building the Golden Dataset: Generate or curate relevant chunks and ideal answers for a Golden Dataset through hand-authoring, LLM-assisted generation, or tools such as DeepEval's synthetic-data generators.
[Component-level evaluation] Evaluating the generator alone: Evaluate the generator independently by providing known-good context and checking whether it produces faithful and relevant answers.
[Component-level evaluation] Detecting unfaithful answers: Detect unfaithful claims, irrelevant answers, missing information, and misuse of provided context.
[Component-level evaluation] Component tests with DeepEval & RAGAS: Implement component tests using frameworks such as DeepEval or RAGAS while understanding what each metric actually measures.
[Pipeline-level evaluation] The full retrieve → generate pipeline: Evaluate the complete retrieval → context → generation pipeline.
[Pipeline-level evaluation] The RAG Triad: Measure the RAG Triad:
[Pipeline-level evaluation] Contextual Relevancy: Contextual Relevancy
[Pipeline-level evaluation] Faithfulness: Faithfulness
[Pipeline-level evaluation] Answer Relevance: Answer Relevance
[Pipeline-level evaluation] When good components interact badly: Understand how individually strong components can still interact poorly when connected.
[Pipeline-level evaluation] Diagnosing pipeline-level failures: Diagnose cases such as high retrieval precision but low overall contextual relevance or poor downstream answers.
[Pipeline-level evaluation] Locating the root failure: Determine whether the root failure lies in retrieval, assembled context, or generation.
[Application-level evaluation] Evaluating from the user's perspective: Evaluate the RAG system from the actual user's perspective rather than only testing internal components.
[Application-level evaluation] Factual correctness: Measure whether the final answer is factually correct given the available evidence.
[Application-level evaluation] Answer completeness: Evaluate completeness: does the answer address all important parts of the user's request?
[Application-level evaluation] Tone, format & citation behaviour: Evaluate application-specific requirements such as tone, style, persona, format, citation behavior, and instruction following.
[Application-level evaluation] Operational metrics per query: Track operational metrics including latency, token usage, cost per query, and error rates alongside quality.
[Safety evaluation for RAG] Harmful & disallowed responses: Evaluate whether the system produces harmful, illegal, dangerous, biased, or otherwise disallowed responses.
[Safety evaluation for RAG] PII protection & redaction: Test whether sensitive PII such as contact details, credentials, or payment information is appropriately protected or redacted.
[Safety evaluation for RAG] Direct & indirect prompt injection: Test direct and indirect prompt injection, including malicious instructions hidden inside retrieved documents.
[Safety evaluation for RAG] Jailbreak attempts: Test jailbreak attempts intended to bypass application guardrails.
[Safety evaluation for RAG] Poisoned retrieval content: Evaluate whether retrieved malicious or misleading content can manipulate the model into leaking data or ignoring application instructions.
Retrieval metrics you actually compute: Recall@k and MRR on a labelled query set.
Faithfulness vs answer relevance: A cited lie and an uncited truth fail different tests.

nodes.title: M7.9 · Agent Evals
nodes.summary: M7.9 in L7 · LLM Evaluations, 19 topics: Six dimensions of agent evaluation; Why the final answer is not enough; Tool selection.
checklist: Six dimensions of agent evaluation: Evaluate agentic systems at the level of decision-making, trajectories, tool usage, task completion, recovery, and safety.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Why the final answer is not enough: Understand why evaluating only the final answer is insufficient when an agent autonomously decides how to complete a task.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Tool selection: Evaluate whether the agent chooses the correct tool for a given situation.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Tool argument correctness: Test whether the agent generates accurate and properly formatted tool arguments.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Trajectory quality: Evaluate the sequence of actions taken by the agent and whether the trajectory is appropriate for the task.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Loops, redundancy & early exit: Detect unnecessary tool calls, redundant actions, loops, incorrect ordering, and premature termination.
[Agent behavior & trajectory evaluation] Task-completion success rate: Measure overall task-completion success rate for complex multi-step user requests.
[Failure recovery] Injecting realistic failures: Introduce tool failures, malformed results, unavailable services, missing information, and unexpected intermediate states.
[Failure recovery] Noticing failure & choosing recovery: Evaluate whether the agent notices failure and chooses an appropriate recovery strategy.
[Failure recovery] Retry, fall back, replan, escalate: Test whether it can retry, select an alternative tool, revise its plan, or escalate appropriately.
[Failure recovery] Measuring recovery, not just success: Measure successful recovery rather than only measuring success in ideal conditions.
[Agent safety evaluation] Unauthorized & destructive actions: Test whether agents attempt unauthorized or destructive actions.
[Agent safety evaluation] Approval gates & permission boundaries: Evaluate human-approval gates and permission boundaries around consequential actions.
[Agent safety evaluation] Resistance to prompt injection: Test agent resistance to direct and indirect prompt injections designed to hijack its tool usage.
[Agent safety evaluation] Secret extraction & scope escape: Attempt to manipulate an agent into revealing secrets, exceeding permissions, or using tools outside the intended scope.

[Agent safety evaluation] Cybersecurity capability benchmarks: Use relevant cybersecurity benchmarks where appropriate to assess dangerous capabilities such as exploitation, reverse engineering, or other high-risk computer-use behavior.
[Agent safety evaluation] Outcome quality vs execution efficiency: Track both outcome quality and execution efficiency through steps, latency, tool calls, token usage, and cost.
Trajectory evals: Score tool choice and arguments, not only the final sentence.
Step-budget violations as failures: An agent that finishes after 40 hops still failed the product.

nodes.title: Level 8 overview: AI Security
nodes.summary: Level 8 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: secure LLM, RAG, and agent systems against model-specific attacks, unsafe actions, data leakage, and regulatory risk.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (5/10): Expect one question, usually about prompt injection, and it’s rarely a deciding factor. Knowing the basics is enough unless you’re applying for security roles.

Why it matters on the job (7/10): Prompt injection and data leaks are real risks in any system that uses tools or private data. One incident can be very costly, but daily effort is moderate unless you’re in a regulated industry.

Goal of this level: Level 8 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: secure LLM, RAG, and agent systems against model-specific attacks, unsafe actions, data leakage, and regulatory risk.

nodes.title: M8.1 · AI threat model
nodes.summary: M8.1 in L8 · AI Security, 7 topics: How the attack surface changes; Trust boundaries; Model output is untrusted.
checklist: How the attack surface changes: Understand how the attack surface changes when models can process untrusted content, access private data, call tools, and take actions.
Trust boundaries: Identify trust boundaries across prompts, retrieved data, tools, memory, model outputs, and external systems.
Model output is untrusted: Treat model-generated outputs and actions as untrusted until validated.
Trust boundaries on a sketch: User, retriever, tools, logs — mark which side is untrusted.
Output is attacker-controlled: Treat model text like user input when it reaches a browser or a shell.
Interview: draw the threat model: Assets, actors, and the one path that combines data, tools and an exit.
Confused deputy as the default: The model will act with your privileges on someone else's words.

nodes.title: M8.2 · Prompt injection & data exfiltration
nodes.summary: M8.2 in L8 · AI Security, 8 topics: Direct vs indirect injection; What injection attacks attempt; Untrusted input + tools + an exit path.
checklist: Direct vs indirect injection: Distinguish direct prompt injection from indirect injection hidden inside documents, web pages, emails, retrieved chunks, or tool outputs.
What injection attacks attempt: Understand attacks that attempt to override instructions, manipulate tools, expose private context, or redirect an agent's objective.
Untrusted input + tools + an exit path: Understand the dangerous combination of untrusted input + powerful tools/private data + an exfiltration path.
Layered defences: Defend using instruction/data separation, least privilege, authorization checks, restricted tools, confirmation gates, and output validation.
Why "ignore malicious instructions" fails: Understand why prompting the model to “ignore malicious instructions” is not a sufficient security boundary.
Indirect injection via retrieved HTML: Hidden text in a page is still a command stream.
No-egress tools as a control: If the model cannot send, it cannot exfiltrate.
Interview: stop an exfil path: Fence data, allow-list, confirm, and keep secrets out of the prompt.

links.title: Level 8 module M8.2: Prompt injection & data exfiltration (source)

nodes.title: M8.3 · Jailbreaks, guardrails & moderation
nodes.summary: M8.3 in L8 · AI Security, 7 topics: Jailbreaks vs injection; Input & output guardrails; Why one layer is not enough.
checklist: Jailbreaks vs injection: Distinguish jailbreaks from prompt injection and recognize common jailbreak patterns.
Input & output guardrails: Add input and output guardrails, moderation, validation, and policy checks.
Why one layer is not enough: Understand the limitations of model-based guardrails and why multiple layers of defense are required.
Testing against obfuscated input: Test guardrails against adversarial and obfuscated inputs instead of only normal requests.
Jailbreak vs injection: Jailbreak is a user trying to drop policy; injection is untrusted data doing it.
Layered filters still fail closed: A block-list is a hint; capability removal is the boundary.
Interview: test obfuscated input: Homoglyphs, other languages, and base64 in the corpus.

links.title: Level 8 module M8.3: Jailbreaks, guardrails & moderation (source)

nodes.title: M8.4 · Agent & tool security
nodes.summary: M8.4 in L8 · AI Security, 8 topics: Least privilege for agents; Read-only vs consequential actions; Validating tool use outside the LLM.
checklist: Least privilege for agents: Apply least privilege so agents only receive the tools and permissions required for the task.
Read-only vs consequential actions: Separate read-only actions from consequential actions such as sending messages, modifying records, deleting data, purchasing, or executing code.
Validating tool use outside the LLM: Validate tool selection, arguments, permissions, and outputs independently of the LLM.
Human approval for irreversible actions: Add human approval for sensitive or irreversible operations.
Step, runtime & cost limits: Limit agent steps, runtime, cost, and tool usage to prevent runaway execution.
Sandboxing generated code: Sandbox model-generated code and treat generated SQL, commands, URLs, or API calls as untrusted.
Tool allow-lists in code: Recipients, URLs and verbs are decided by the server.
Human approval as a product feature: Show the draft action and wait; do not auto-send.

links.title: Level 8 module M8.4: Agent & tool security (source)

nodes.title: M8.5 · RAG & knowledge security
nodes.summary: M8.5 in L8 · AI Security, 8 topics: Retrieved documents are data, not instructions; Retrieval poisoning; Document-level permissions.
checklist: Retrieved documents are data, not instructions: Treat retrieved documents as untrusted data, not trusted instructions.
Retrieval poisoning: Understand retrieval poisoning and malicious instructions hidden inside indexed documents.
Document-level permissions: Enforce document-level permissions so users retrieve only information they are authorized to access.
Preventing cross-tenant leakage: Prevent cross-user or cross-tenant data leakage from vector stores and memory systems.
Preserving provenance: Preserve source/provenance information for retrieved content.
Per-document ACLs at retrieve time: Filter before ANN, not after the model saw the text.
Poisoned corpus as a first-class threat: An insider or a public page can rewrite behaviour.
Interview: tenant isolation: Separate indexes or mandatory tenant filters you cannot forget.

links.title: Level 8 module M8.5: RAG & knowledge security (source)

nodes.title: M8.6 · Data privacy, PII & secrets
nodes.summary: M8.6 in L8 · AI Security, 8 topics: Identifying sensitive data; Redaction & minimization; Keeping PII out of logs & traces.
checklist: Identifying sensitive data: Identify sensitive data including PII, credentials, financial information, private conversations, and confidential business data.
Redaction & minimization: Detect, redact, mask, or minimize sensitive information before sending it to models when appropriate.
Keeping PII out of logs & traces: Avoid unnecessarily storing sensitive data in prompts, logs, traces, memories, vector stores, or evaluation datasets.
Retention, deletion & residency: Understand data retention, deletion, residency, access control, and third-party model-provider considerations.

Private connectivity & zero retention: Use the controls that make regulated deployments possible: private connectivity to the model endpoint, no public egress, and contractual zero-retention or no-training terms.
Protecting secrets from the model: Protect secrets so they are never unnecessarily exposed to the model.
PII in traces: Redact before the log shipper; retention is a legal setting.
Zero-retention vendor options: Know what the provider stores and for how long.

links.title: Level 8 module M8.6: Data privacy, PII & secrets (source)

nodes.title: M8.7 · Red teaming AI systems
nodes.summary: M8.7 in L8 · AI Security, 8 topics: Building adversarial test suites; Attacking RAG through the corpus; Attacking agents through their tools.
checklist: Building adversarial test suites: Build adversarial tests for prompt injection, jailbreaks, malicious documents, tool misuse, data extraction, and unsafe agent actions.
Attacking RAG through the corpus: Test RAG systems by injecting malicious content into retrievable documents.
Attacking agents through their tools: Test agents by attempting to make them exceed permissions, misuse tools, reveal secrets, or enter loops.
Vulnerabilities become regression tests: Turn discovered vulnerabilities into permanent security regression tests.
Attack-success & leakage rates: Track measures such as attack-success rate, sensitive-data leakage, and unsafe-action rate where useful.
A living attack suite: Each new jailbreak becomes a regression case.
Success rate, not anecdotes: Report how many of 50 attacks landed, with the control that stopped them.
Interview: your red-team loop: Enumerate assets, attack, patch in code, add a test, re-run.

nodes.summary: M8.8 in L8 · AI Security, 7 topics: Bias, transparency & human oversight; Documenting use, limits & risks; The EU AI Act & India's DPDP.
checklist: Bias, transparency & human oversight: Understand core concerns around hallucination, bias/fairness, transparency, accountability, and human oversight.
Documenting use, limits & risks: Document intended use, known limitations, important risks, evaluations, and human-control mechanisms.
The EU AI Act & India's DPDP: Understand the practical implications of relevant regulations such as the EU AI Act and India's DPDP framework.
Auditability: Maintain auditability through model/prompt versions, logs, approvals, and evaluation records.
Audit logs without bodies: Store who, what, when — not the full user text if policy forbids it.
A disclosure you can stand behind: Limits, human oversight, and where data goes.
Interview: EU AI Act vs DPDP in one minute: Risk class and documentation vs consent and purpose limitation.

nodes.title: M9.1 · The AI system design framework
nodes.summary: M9.1 in L9 · AI System Design, 7 topics: Starting from requirements & constraints; Prompting, RAG, agents or fine-tuning; Quality ↔ latency ↔ cost.
checklist: Starting from requirements & constraints: Start from the use case, success criteria, constraints, traffic, latency requirements, quality requirements, privacy, and cost budget.
Prompting, RAG, agents or fine-tuning: Decide deliberately between prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, or combinations of them.
Quality ↔ latency ↔ cost: Reason about the central trade-offs: quality ↔ latency ↔ cost, plus complexity and reliability.
Baseline before sophistication: Establish a simple baseline before introducing sophisticated architecture.
Constraints before components: Latency, cost, privacy and audit beat a fashionable diagram.
Baseline, then one sophistication: Ship retrieve-and-generate before agents or graphs.

checklist: Where knowledge should come from: Decide what knowledge should come from model knowledge, prompt/context, RAG, memory, or external tools.
The full context pipeline: Design the full context pipeline: ingestion → retrieval → reranking → context assembly → generation.
Combining retrieval approaches: Combine vector, keyword, graph, and other retrieval approaches where justified.
Freshness, access control & provenance: Handle freshness, updates, access control, scale, and source provenance.
Retrieved dynamically or held in context: Decide what information should be retrieved dynamically versus kept permanently in the model's context or external state.
Freshness SLAs on knowledge: Who updates the corpus and how stale is allowed.
Access control as architecture: Retrieval is a security boundary, not a helper.
Interview: where knowledge lives: Prompt, index, database, or fine-tune — and why not the others.

nodes.title: M9.3 · Model routing & gateways
nodes.summary: M9.3 in L9 · AI System Design, 8 topics: What a model gateway does; Routing on task, cost & risk; Model cascades.
checklist: What a model gateway does: Understand the role of a model gateway as the abstraction between application code and model providers.
Routing on task, cost & risk: Route requests based on task type, capability, latency, context length, cost, modality, or risk.
Model cascades: Build model cascades where cheaper/faster models handle easy requests and stronger models handle difficult ones.
Provider fallbacks & quality risk: Add model/provider fallbacks and understand the quality risks introduced by switching models.
Centralising auth, limits & tracking: Centralize authentication, usage tracking, retries, rate limits, and provider abstraction where appropriate.
A cascade that fails open to a safe default: Cheap model first; escalate; never silently drop the schema.
Central auth and quotas: The gateway is where keys and budgets live, not in each service.
Interview: design a gateway: Route, fallback, log usage, pin snapshots, and hide keys from apps.

nodes.title: M9.4 · Latency & inference optimization
nodes.summary: M9.4 in L9 · AI System Design, 8 topics: Breaking latency into components; Streaming for perceived latency; Parallelising independent work.
checklist: Breaking latency into components: Break latency into components such as retrieval, TTFT, model generation, tool calls, and network overhead.
Streaming for perceived latency: Use streaming to improve perceived latency.
Parallelising independent work: Parallelize independent operations and avoid unnecessary sequential LLM calls.
When a smaller model will do: Understand when smaller/faster models can replace larger models.
Context reduction & batching: Apply prompt/context reduction, batching, and inference-service optimizations where appropriate.
Throughput & utilization at scale: Reason about throughput, latency, and utilization at scale.
Streaming as perceived latency: Users forgive a long total if the first token is fast.
Prefill vs decode costs: Long prompts hurt TTFT; long outputs hurt tokens and time.

links.title: Level 9 module M9.4: Latency & inference optimization (source)

nodes.title: M9.5 · Caching architecture
nodes.summary: M9.5 in L9 · AI System Design, 8 topics: The four caches in an AI system; What is safe to cache; Semantic caching.
checklist: The four caches in an AI system: Understand the different caches available in an AI system: exact-response caching, prompt/context caching, retrieval caching, and semantic caching.
What is safe to cache: Decide what is safe to cache and define appropriate expiration/invalidation strategies.
Semantic caching: Use semantic caching when different queries can reasonably share an answer.
Freshness vs latency & cost: Understand the trade-off between freshness, quality, latency, and cost.
Measuring the hit rate: Measure actual cache hit rate and savings rather than assuming caching helps.
Semantic cache invalidation: A new policy doc must bust similar questions, not just exact matches.
What you must never cache: Personalized or secret answers in a shared key.
Interview: four caches: HTTP, prompt prefix, retrieval, and semantic — plus one thing each must not store.

nodes.title: M9.6 · Reliability, guardrails & graceful degradation
nodes.summary: M9.6 in L9 · AI System Design, 8 topics: Designing for every failure; Timeouts, circuit breakers & queues; Guardrails at system boundaries.
checklist: Designing for every failure: Design for model failures, provider outages, tool failures, rate limits, malformed outputs, and retrieval failures.
Timeouts, circuit breakers & queues: Add timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, queues, and rate limits where appropriate.
Guardrails at system boundaries: Place guardrails at important system boundaries rather than relying entirely on the model.
Graceful degradation: Design graceful degradation: simpler model, reduced functionality, cached answer, human escalation, or explicit inability to complete the request.
Human approval for high-risk actions: Use human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions.
Service-level expectations: Define service-level expectations for availability, latency, and quality.
Degrade to search or a form: A down model should not take the whole product with it.
SLOs you can actually page on: Error rate and p95, not 'the vibe dropped'.

links.title: Level 9 module M9.6: Reliability, guardrails & graceful degradation (source)

nodes.summary: M9.7 in L9 · AI System Design, 8 topics: The end-to-end flow; Deterministic vs model-delegated decisions; Sync, async, queued or long-running.
checklist: The end-to-end flow: Design the end-to-end flow between retrieval, models, tools, agents, guardrails, caches, and external systems.
Deterministic vs model-delegated decisions: Decide which decisions should be deterministic and which should be delegated to the model.
Sync, async, queued or long-running: Choose between synchronous execution, asynchronous jobs, queues, and long-running agent workflows.
Avoiding unnecessary agentic complexity: Avoid unnecessary agentic complexity when a deterministic pipeline is sufficient.
Component boundaries: Define clear component boundaries so individual parts can be changed, evaluated, and scaled independently.
Sync for the user path, queue for the rest: Embeddings and evals do not belong on the request thread.
Avoiding an agent for a flowchart: If you can draw the branches, code the branches.
Interview: orchestrate a pipeline: Ingest async, retrieve sync, generate streamed, evaluate offline.

Failures become evaluation cases: Turn production failures and user feedback into new evaluation cases.
Versioning for traceable regressions: Version models, prompts, retrieval configurations, and application changes so regressions can be traced.
Deploy → observe → improve → redeploy: Understand the loop: deploy → observe → collect feedback → evaluate → improve → redeploy.
Implicit feedback: Edits, regenerates and abandoned answers are labels.
A weekly improve loop: Mine failures, add cases, ship a prompt, watch online.

Application vs model LLMOps: Distinguish application LLMOps, which runs products on top of existing models, from model LLMOps, which trains and hosts the models themselves, and recognize that most teams practise the first.

Why LLM systems are hard to operate: Understand what makes LLM systems harder to operate: non-deterministic outputs, prompts that change behavior without a code change, provider-side model updates, and a cost attached to every request.

What a release consists of: Define what a release actually is for an LLM application: code, prompts, model version, retrieval configuration, index contents, and tool definitions, all of which must be versioned together.

Operating RAG vs agents: Understand how operating a RAG application differs from operating an agent, from stale indexes and retrieval drift on one side to runaway loops and tool failures on the other.
The lifecycle of this level: Map the lifecycle this level follows: track → evaluate → guard → serve → ship → deploy → monitor → improve.
What is non-deterministic in the loop: Prompts, models, and judges — pin and record all three.
Human review as an LLMOps stage: Not every change is a silent deploy.

nodes.title: M10.2 · Preparing your apps for production
nodes.summary: M10.2 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 8 topics: Reuse your Level 4 and 5 apps; Configuration, not code; Pinned model & dependency versions.
checklist: Reuse your Level 4 and 5 apps: Take the RAG application from Level 4 and the agent from Level 5 as the two systems this level operates, rather than building new ones.
Configuration, not code: Separate configuration from code, so the model, prompts, retrieval parameters, and tool set can change without a rewrite.
Pinned model & dependency versions: Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today.
Traceable from the first request: Make each request traceable from the start by attaching a request ID, the prompt version, and the model version to everything it touches.
The Level 7 eval set as yardstick: Carry the evaluation dataset from Level 7 forward as the fixed yardstick every later change will be measured against.
Feature flags on prompts: Flip back without a rebuild.
Contract tests on the output schema: Break the build when a field disappears.

nodes.title: M10.3 · Experiment tracking & prompt versioning
nodes.summary: M10.3 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 11 topics: Experiments in MLflow; Scores, prompts & outputs per run; Comparing runs.
checklist: [Tracking experiments] Experiments in MLflow: Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set.
[Tracking experiments] Scores, prompts & outputs per run: Log evaluation scores as metrics and keep prompts, configurations, and sample outputs as artifacts of the run.
[Tracking experiments] Comparing runs: Compare runs side by side to see which change actually moved quality, latency, or cost.
[Tracking experiments] A baseline before changes: Record a baseline run for both applications before changing anything.
[Versioning prompts] A prompt registry: Store prompts in a prompt registry such as Langfuse, so they are versioned, reviewed, and deployed independently of code.
[Versioning prompts] Staging & production labels: Label prompt versions for staging and production, and promote a version by moving the label rather than editing text in place.
[Versioning prompts] Runtime fetch with a fallback: Fetch prompts at runtime with caching and a pinned fallback, so a registry outage does not take the application down.
[Versioning prompts] Rollback by moving a label: Roll back a bad prompt by moving the production label back to the previous version.
[Versioning prompts] Traces linked to prompt versions: Link every trace to the prompt version that produced it, so a regression can be traced to the change that caused it.
Dataset versioning: The golden set is as important as the prompt.
Promotion rules: Dev to staging to prod with the same eval command.

nodes.title: M10.4 · Evaluation as a release gate
nodes.summary: M10.4 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 10 topics: The eval suite as DeepEval tests; RAG & agent metrics; Per-metric thresholds.
checklist: [Wiring the suite into the build] The eval suite as DeepEval tests: Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner.

[Wiring the suite into the build] RAG & agent metrics: Score the RAG application on faithfulness, answer relevance, and contextual precision, and the agent on tool selection, task completion, and step efficiency.
[Wiring the suite into the build] Per-metric thresholds: Set a threshold per metric against the recorded baseline, and fail the build when a change falls below it.
[Wiring the suite into the build] Reviewed synthetic cases: Extend coverage with synthetic test cases generated by DeepEval, reviewed by a person before they join the suite.
[Making the gate trustworthy] Handling non-determinism: Handle non-determinism by repeating runs, using tolerance bands, and fixing sampling settings where the task allows it.
[Making the gate trustworthy] Fast subset vs full suite: Budget evaluation cost and time by running a fast subset on every change and the full suite before release.
[Making the gate trustworthy] Prompt & model changes gated too: Treat a prompt change, a model change, and a retrieval change exactly like a code change, so all of them pass through the same gate.
[Making the gate trustworthy] Gated runs logged in MLflow: Record every gated run in MLflow, so the history of a metric shows which release moved it.
Canary a prompt to 5 percent: Watch quality and cost before a full flip.
Shadow a new model: Score it on live traffic without showing the user.

nodes.title: M10.5 · Runtime guardrails
nodes.summary: M10.5 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 10 topics: Level 8 threats as runtime checks; Schema validation & re-asking; Topical rails with NeMo Guardrails.
checklist: [Validating inputs and outputs] Level 8 threats as runtime checks: Turn the threat model from Level 8 into runtime checks that run on every request, in front of and behind the model.
[Validating inputs and outputs] Schema validation & re-asking: Enforce structured outputs with Guardrails AI, validating against a schema and re-asking the model when validation fails.
[Validating inputs and outputs] Topical rails with NeMo Guardrails: Define topical and conversational rails with NeMo Guardrails, and understand when that framework suits better than a validator.
[Validating inputs and outputs] Input & output checks: Check inputs for prompt injection attempts and personal data, and outputs for ungrounded claims, off-topic answers, and leaked secrets.

[Limiting agents and measuring the guards] Agent tool, step & spend limits: Validate tool arguments before execution, and cap agent steps, retries, and spend per request so a loop cannot run unbounded.
[Limiting agents and measuring the guards] Guardrail latency & false positives: Measure what each guardrail costs in latency and how often it blocks a legitimate request.
[Limiting agents and measuring the guards] Logging every block: Log every block and every re-ask, so guardrail behavior can be reviewed and tuned rather than trusted blindly.
Input and output filters as code: Policy is not only a system prompt.
Rate limits per user and per tool: Abuse is an LLMOps problem too.
Interview: a runtime guardrail: Schema, allow-list, PII redact, and a hard deny path.

nodes.title: M10.6 · Application serving & containerization
nodes.summary: M10.6 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 11 topics: A FastAPI backend; Streaming with server-sent events; Timeouts & disconnects.
checklist: [A production backend] A FastAPI backend: Move application logic out of notebooks and scripts into a FastAPI backend with validated requests and typed responses.
[A production backend] Streaming with server-sent events: Stream responses token by token with server-sent events, so users see the answer forming instead of waiting for all of it.
[A production backend] Timeouts & disconnects: Set timeouts and handle client disconnects, so an abandoned request stops consuming model tokens.
[A production backend] Health & readiness endpoints: Expose health and readiness endpoints that report whether the model provider and vector database are reachable.
[A thin frontend] A thin Streamlit frontend: Build a Streamlit frontend that only renders the interface and calls the backend, holding no application logic of its own.
[A thin frontend] Showing streams & errors: Render the streamed response and surface errors, timeouts, and guardrail blocks to the user in plain language.
[Containers] Docker images: Package the backend and frontend as Docker images with small, reproducible builds.
[Containers] The stack in Docker Compose: Run the backend, frontend, and the vector database your RAG application already uses together with Docker Compose.
[Containers] Secrets at runtime, not in images: Supply secrets and API keys through the environment at runtime, never baked into an image.
Prompt vs model vs data change: Isolate which one moved the metric.
Reproducible runs: Same snapshot, same set, same seed policy.

nodes.summary: M10.7 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 8 topics: Tests → eval gate → build; Commit-tagged images; Pipeline secrets.
checklist: Tests → eval gate → build: Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order.
Commit-tagged images: Tag every image with the commit it was built from, and push only images that passed the gate to a registry such as Docker Hub.
Pipeline secrets: Store provider keys and registry credentials as pipeline secrets, and keep them out of logs and pull-request builds from forks.
Manual approval for production: Require a manual approval before a release reaches production, while allowing staging to deploy automatically.
Rollback to a known tag: Keep the previous image deployable, so a rollback is a redeploy of a known tag rather than a rebuild.
Eval in GitHub Actions: A required check, not a manual notebook.
Secrets in OIDC, not in logs: Keys never appear in action output.

nodes.title: M10.8 · Deployment on AWS
nodes.summary: M10.8 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 10 topics: EC2 with an IAM role; Secrets Manager; Releases with CodeDeploy.
checklist: [Servers, identity and secrets] EC2 with an IAM role: Provision EC2 instances for the application, install Docker, and attach an IAM role instead of storing access keys on the machine.
[Servers, identity and secrets] Secrets Manager: Store provider API keys in AWS Secrets Manager and load them when the container starts.
[Automated releases] Releases with CodeDeploy: Use AWS CodeDeploy to pull a tagged image and replace running containers, with health checks deciding whether the release continues.
[Automated releases] In-place vs blue/green: Choose between in-place and blue/green releases, and roll back automatically when the new version fails its health checks.
[Traffic and scale] Load balancer & streaming timeouts: Put an Application Load Balancer in front of the instances, and raise its idle timeout so long streamed responses are not cut off.
[Traffic and scale] Auto Scaling groups: Add an Auto Scaling group that adds instances when busy and removes them when quiet.
[Traffic and scale] Scale on concurrency, not CPU: Scale on request concurrency rather than CPU, since an LLM application spends most of its time waiting on the model provider.
[Traffic and scale] Provider rate limits cap first: Recognize that provider rate limits usually cap throughput before your servers do, and size scaling with those limits in view.
Rollback that includes the prompt id: Reverting the container is not enough.
Incident notes without user text: Timeline, impact, and the pin you restored.

nodes.title: M10.9 · Monitoring & observability
nodes.summary: M10.9 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 10 topics: Prometheus & Node Exporter; Application metrics; Grafana dashboards.
checklist: [Infrastructure and application metrics] Prometheus & Node Exporter: Run Prometheus to collect metrics from every instance, using Node Exporter for CPU, memory, disk, and network.
[Infrastructure and application metrics] Application metrics: Export application metrics from the backend: requests, latency percentiles, errors, model calls, tokens, and guardrail blocks.
[Dashboards and alerts] Grafana dashboards: Build Grafana dashboards that show server health, traffic, latency, error rate, and token spend side by side.
[Dashboards and alerts] Alerts that need a human: Alert on the signals that need a human, such as error-rate spikes, latency beyond budget, failed scaling, and spend above a daily limit.
[Tracing and online evaluation] Tracing in Langfuse: Trace every request in Langfuse through retrieval, model calls, and tool calls, with latency and cost recorded at each step.
[Tracing and online evaluation] Online evals & user feedback: Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them.
[Tracing and online evaluation] Failures back into the suite: Turn production failures found in traces and feedback into new cases for the Level 7 evaluation suite.
Quality dashboards next to SRE: Faithfulness and cost sit beside p95.
Trace-to-example: One click from a bad answer to an eval case.
Interview: what you watch in week one: Traffic, errors, tokens, and a weekly sampled review.

nodes.title: M10.10 · Capstone: LLMOps Project
nodes.summary: M10.10 in L10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production, 7 topics: LLM-specific incidents; The lever for each cause; Runbooks.
checklist: LLM-specific incidents: Recognize the incidents specific to LLM applications: a provider outage, a silent model update, a prompt regression, a stale index, a runaway agent, and a cost spike.
The lever for each cause: Respond with the lever that matches the cause: a model fallback, a prompt rollback, an image rollback, an index rebuild, or a spend cap.
Runbooks: Write a short runbook per incident type, naming the signal that detects it, the first action to take, and the person who decides.
Re-evaluate on model changes: Re-run the evaluation suite whenever the provider announces a model change, before the change reaches your users.
Blameless reviews: Run a blameless review after each incident, and add the case that caused it to the evaluation suite.
The capstone ops story: How you would page, roll back, and add the miss to the set.
A runbook one page long: Prompt id, model pin, eval command, and who to call.

nodes.title: Level 11 overview: Managed AI Platforms
nodes.summary: Level 11 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Ship an AI application on the platforms teams actually buy — a cloud provider's managed platform, an open-weight hosting provider, or a router spanning several — and know which parts to hand over and which to keep.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (6/10): Matters a lot at enterprises and IT services companies, where Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, or Vertex experience is often a hard filter. At startups it matters much less.
Why it matters on the job (7/10): Often required, since companies frequently run AI inside their existing cloud for compliance. You mostly learn the specific platform on the job.
Prerequisites: Level 9 · AI System Design  Level 10 · LLMOps: From Development to Production

Goal of this level: Level 11 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Ship an AI application on the platforms teams actually buy — a cloud provider's managed platform, an open-weight hosting provider, or a router spanning several — and know which parts to hand over and which to keep.
Plan 9 modules and the capstone “deploy on a managed platform” before moving on

nodes.title: M11.1 · The three ways to consume a model
nodes.summary: M11.1 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 9 topics: Three ways to consume a model; Open weights without running GPUs; Why regulated teams cannot use a public API.
checklist: Three ways to consume a model: Understand the three paths an organization can take: a provider's public API, a managed platform inside its own cloud account, or open weights it hosts itself or through an inference provider.
Open weights without running GPUs: Recognize that open weights no longer imply operating GPUs, since managed platforms and inference providers serve the same open models on demand.
Why regulated teams cannot use a public API: Understand why most regulated organizations cannot use a public API directly, and why that constraint decides architecture long before quality does.
Comparing the three paths: Compare the three paths on identity, data handling, region, capacity, price per token, operational effort, and how quickly new models reach you.

Platform, gateway, or both: Understand where a managed platform sits relative to the model gateway pattern: it can be your gateway, sit behind one, or be one provider among several that a gateway routes to.
Decision matrix for a new workload: Score public API versus managed platform versus self-host on data class, region, latency and ops headcount.
Switching cost after month one: List what you would have to rebuild if you leave each path after a quarter.
Pick a path under constraints: Walk through a regulated team that cannot send prompts to a public API and name the path you would choose.
Hybrid path in practice: Use a public API for prototypes and a managed platform for production of the same prompt.

nodes.title: M11.2 · Platform anatomy: Bedrock, Vertex AI & Azure AI Foundry
nodes.summary: M11.2 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 11 topics: The shape all three share; Reading a model catalog; Invoking through the platform.
checklist: [What a managed platform gives you] The shape all three share: Understand the shape all three share: a catalog of closed and open-weight models, one endpoint style, one identity system, one network boundary, and one bill.

[What a managed platform gives you] Reading a model catalog: Read a platform's model catalog the way you read a model card, noting which providers are offered, which regions carry them, and which versions are pinned or retired.

[What a managed platform gives you] Invoking through the platform: Understand how invocation differs from a provider SDK, including the platform's own request format, its converse-style unified API, and the provider-native passthrough where one exists.

[What a managed platform gives you] Same ideas, different vocabulary: Recognize the platform-specific vocabulary for the same ideas, so a Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Azure AI Foundry document reads as a variation rather than a new subject.
[Working on one platform] Calling a hosted model: Call a hosted model on one platform from application code and confirm the response, usage, and cost reporting you get back.
[Working on one platform] Swapping models inside one catalog: Compare the same prompt across two models in the same catalog without changing how you authenticate, network, or bill.
[Working on one platform] What the platform does not give you: Understand what the platform does not give you: prompt quality, retrieval design, evaluation depth, and product behavior remain yours.
Pinning a model version: Record the exact model id and date; never float to latest in production.
Catalog deprecation watch: Subscribe to retirement notices and keep a second model already evaluated.
Converse versus native passthrough: Know when the unified API hides a feature you need and when to use the vendor payload.
One call on three platforms: Sketch the same chat request on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry and name the identity and region knobs.
