nodes.title: M11.3 · Identity, networking & tenancy
nodes.summary: M11.3 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 10 topics: Cloud identity instead of API keys; Least privilege for model access; Auditing who invoked what.
checklist: [Identity and access] Cloud identity instead of API keys: Replace API keys with cloud identity: roles, service accounts, and workload identity that grant a service the right to invoke a model.
[Identity and access] Least privilege for model access: Apply least privilege to model access, scoping which models, regions, and actions an application or team may use.
[Identity and access] Auditing who invoked what: Understand how platform access is audited, and why an audit trail of who invoked which model matters in regulated environments.

[Network boundary and tenancy] Private connectivity, no public egress: Reach a model over private connectivity so requests never traverse the public internet, and understand what that buys you and what it costs.

[Network boundary and tenancy] Tenant isolation on shared infrastructure: Design tenant isolation on a shared platform: separate accounts or projects, scoped credentials, per-tenant keys, and retrieval that cannot cross a tenant boundary.
[Network boundary and tenancy] Encryption & customer-managed keys: Understand encryption and key management options, including customer-managed keys for data at rest.
Workload identity for a worker: Bind a job or pod to a role that can invoke only the named models it needs.
Cross-tenant prompt leak tests: Prove that retrieval and logs cannot return another tenant's text.
Key rotation without downtime: Rotate a customer-managed key and confirm in-flight calls still succeed.
Private link failure mode: Know what happens when the private endpoint is down and whether a public fallback is allowed.

links.title: Level 11 module M11.3: Identity, networking & tenancy (source)

nodes.title: M11.4 · Regions, residency & compliance
nodes.summary: M11.4 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 9 topics: Models exist per region; Data residency & localization; Retention & training terms in writing.
checklist: Models exist per region: Understand that a model exists in specific regions, and that the region you are permitted to use often decides which models you may design around.
Data residency & localization: Plan for data residency requirements, including Indian data-localization expectations and the sector rules that sit above them.
Retention & training terms in writing: Understand retention and training terms in writing: what the platform logs, for how long, who can see it, and whether your data may be used to improve a model.
Connecting back to governance: Connect these controls to the governance work of Level 8, where residency, deletion, and third-party processing were named as requirements.

When your model is not in your region: Handle the common case where the model you want is unavailable in your required region, through cross-region reasoning, a different model, or an exception you can document.
Prompt and log residency: Confirm where prompts, completions and traces are stored, not only where inference runs.
Cross-region inference exceptions: Write the exception, the compensating control and the expiry date when you must leave region.
Training-opt-out evidence: Keep the contract clause and console setting that prove your data is not used to train.
Sector overlay for finance or health: Name the extra residency and logging rules a bank or hospital would add.

links.title: Level 11 module M11.4: Regions, residency & compliance (source)

nodes.title: M11.5 · Capacity, quotas & cost
nodes.summary: M11.5 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 12 topics: On-demand vs provisioned throughput; Reading the quota model; Planning for burst traffic.
checklist: [Capacity] On-demand vs provisioned throughput: Distinguish on-demand capacity from provisioned or reserved throughput, and understand why committed capacity changes both price and rate limits.
[Capacity] Reading the quota model: Read the quota model of a platform: requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent requests, and per-model limits that differ by region.
[Capacity] Planning for burst traffic: Plan for burst traffic with queueing, backpressure, and batch endpoints instead of assuming the platform will absorb a spike.
[Capacity] Defending a quota increase: Request and defend a quota increase with traffic evidence, since capacity is an approval process rather than a setting.
[Cost] Cost per request, end to end: Model cost per request end to end, including input and output tokens, retrieval calls, and any managed component you invoke along the way.
[Cost] Attributing spend per team or tenant: Attribute cost to a project, team, or tenant using the platform's own tagging and billing views, which a shared API key cannot do.
[Cost] Budgets & runaway-cost alerts: Set budgets and alerts so a runaway agent loop is caught by spend monitoring rather than by the monthly invoice.
[Cost] Which pricing model wins at your volume: Compare on-demand, committed, and self-hosted economics at your actual volume rather than at the volume in the pricing example.
Tokens-per-minute versus requests-per-minute: Know which limit you will hit first for long-context versus chatty agents.
Provisioned throughput break-even: Compute the daily tokens where reserved capacity beats on-demand.
Queue depth as a product signal: Expose queue wait to the client instead of letting retries stampede the quota.
Cost anomaly playbook: Write the first three checks when spend doubles overnight: loop, cache miss, model swap.

links.title: Level 11 module M11.5: Capacity, quotas & cost (source)

nodes.title: M11.6 · Open-weight model platforms
nodes.summary: M11.6 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 14 topics: The open-weight hosting ladder; Model hubs & checkpoint trust; Serverless inference providers.
checklist: [Where open weights actually run] The open-weight hosting ladder: Understand the spectrum between calling an API and operating hardware: model hubs, serverless inference providers, GPU compute platforms, and your own servers.

[Where open weights actually run] Model hubs & checkpoint trust: Use a model hub such as Hugging Face to find open-weight models, read their cards, check licences and gated access, and judge whether a checkpoint is trustworthy.

[Where open weights actually run] Serverless inference providers: Call an open-weight model through a serverless inference provider such as Together, Fireworks, Groq, or Replicate, where you pay per token and never see a GPU.

[Where open weights actually run] GPU compute platforms: Understand what a GPU compute platform such as Modal, Baseten, or RunPod adds: you bring the serving stack and they schedule, scale, and bill the hardware.

[Where open weights actually run] Serving it yourself with vLLM: Serve a model yourself with vLLM, TGI, or Ollama, and understand continuous batching, KV-cache reuse, and why a naive request loop wastes most of a GPU.

[Choosing and paying for open-weight serving] Per-token vs per-GPU-hour: Compare per-token pricing with per-GPU-hour pricing, and find the utilization point at which renting hardware becomes cheaper than paying per token.
[Choosing and paying for open-weight serving] Cold starts & scale-to-zero: Understand cold starts and scale-to-zero, and why a deployment that idles cheaply may answer its first request slowly.

[Choosing and paying for open-weight serving] Sizing hardware for a model: Size hardware for a model from parameter count, precision, quantization, and KV-cache growth with context length, since memory decides which GPU you need.

[Choosing and paying for open-weight serving] What hosting open weights buys: Understand what hosting open weights gives you — predictable cost at volume, data that never leaves your boundary, and full control of versions — and what it asks of you in return.
[Choosing and paying for open-weight serving] Open vs closed on your own task: Evaluate an open-weight model against a closed one on your own task before assuming that either is obviously better.
Licence and gating checks: Read the model card for licence, acceptable use and gated access before you ship.
KV-cache memory math: Estimate KV-cache bytes from layers, heads, context length and batch before picking a GPU.
Quantization versus quality on your eval: Measure 8-bit and 4-bit against the same held-out set, not a blog number.
Serving SLO for a self-hosted model: Set p95 latency and error budget the same way you would for a managed API.

nodes.title: M11.7 · Model routers & LLM gateways
nodes.summary: M11.7 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 14 topics: One endpoint, many providers; Hosted routers vs self-hosted proxies; Routing rules & automatic failover.
checklist: [What a router is for] One endpoint, many providers: Understand a gateway as one endpoint in front of many providers: it holds the credentials, accepts one request format, and hides which model actually served the request.

[What a router is for] Hosted routers vs self-hosted proxies: Compare hosted routers such as OpenRouter and Portkey with self-hosted proxies such as LiteLLM, and with the routing built into cloud platforms and framework gateways.

[What a router is for] Routing rules & automatic failover: Route by rule — task type, cost ceiling, context length, latency target, region, or risk — and fail over automatically when a provider errors or throttles.

[What a router is for] Virtual keys, budgets & quotas: Use a gateway's spend controls: virtual keys per team or per feature, budgets, quotas, and per-key rate limits that stop one client exhausting shared capacity.
[What a router is for] One view of usage and cost: Get one view of usage, latency, errors, and cost across every provider instead of stitching separate dashboards together.

[Operating a router] The router is on the critical path: Understand the failure mode you have introduced, since a gateway now sits on the critical path and needs its own availability, timeouts, and a bypass plan.

[Operating a router] Differences a router cannot hide: Handle the provider differences a gateway cannot hide: tool-calling formats, structured-output support, token limits, and prompts that behave differently on each model.
[Operating a router] Caching at the gateway: Cache at the gateway, both exact-match and semantic, and decide which requests must never be answered from a cache.

[Operating a router] When a router earns its place: Decide when a router earns its place — several providers, several teams, or spend worth governing — and when one provider and a client library is the honest answer.
[Operating a router] Routing changes who answers: Keep evals in the loop, because a routing rule change swaps the model answering your users without a single line of application code changing.
Failover that preserves tools: Test that a fallback model still accepts the same tool schema or strip tools on failover.
Semantic cache exclusion list: Never cache auth, payments or any request that embeds a secret.
Router canary on evals: Run the eval suite against the routed mix, not only against each model in isolation.
Bypass plan for a dead gateway: Keep a signed-off direct-provider path for incidents.

nodes.title: M11.8 · Managed building blocks: build or buy
nodes.summary: M11.8 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 14 topics: Managed retrieval & knowledge bases; Managed retrieval vs your own stack; Managed agent & workflow runtimes.
checklist: [Retrieval and agents] Managed retrieval & knowledge bases: Understand managed retrieval offerings such as knowledge bases and enterprise search, which package ingestion, chunking, embedding, and retrieval behind a configuration.

[Retrieval and agents] Managed retrieval vs your own stack: Compare a managed knowledge base with the retrieval stack you built in Level 4 on control over chunking, retrieval tuning, evaluation depth, and cost at your corpus size.

[Retrieval and agents] Managed agent & workflow runtimes: Understand managed agent and workflow runtimes, and what they assume about tools, memory, and orchestration compared with the agents you built in Level 5.

[Safety, evaluation and adaptation] Managed guardrails: Understand managed guardrails for content filtering, topic restriction, and sensitive-data redaction, and where they sit relative to your own checks.
[Safety, evaluation and adaptation] Managed evaluation: Understand managed evaluation offerings and judge whether their metrics answer the questions your eval suite from Level 7 was built to answer.

[Safety, evaluation and adaptation] Managed fine-tuning & distillation: Understand managed fine-tuning and distillation, including which base models can be adapted, where the resulting weights live, and whether you can take them with you.
[Deciding, layer by layer] Deciding layer by layer: Decide each layer separately, since adopting a managed retrieval service does not commit you to managed agents, guardrails, or evaluation.

[Deciding, layer by layer] What to judge each candidate on: Judge each candidate on control, transparency, evaluation depth, cost at your volume, and how much of the behavior you must be able to explain to an auditor.

[Deciding, layer by layer] Measuring the portability cost: Measure the portability cost before adopting: a prompt moves between providers in minutes, while a knowledge base, agent, or guardrail configuration usually does not.

[Deciding, layer by layer] When buying is the honest call: Recognize the honest cases for buying: a small team, a standard use case, a compliance deadline, or a workload whose quality bar the managed component already clears.
Exit test for a knowledge base: Time how long it takes to export chunks, embeddings and metadata to your own store.
Guardrail false-positive budget: Measure how often the managed filter blocks an allowed support answer.
Fine-tune portability: Confirm whether adapter weights leave the platform and which runtimes can load them.
Build-versus-buy scorecard: Score control, eval depth, cost at 10x volume and auditor explainability on one page.

links.title: Level 11 module M11.8: Managed building blocks: build or buy (source)

nodes.title: M11.9 · Capstone: deploy on a managed platform
nodes.summary: M11.9 in Level 11 (Managed AI Platforms), 11 topics: What travels and what does not; Keeping an abstraction in place; The real costs of lock-in.
checklist: [Designing for exit] What travels and what does not: Separate what is portable from what is not: prompts, evals, and application code travel easily, while managed indexes, agent definitions, and platform-specific APIs do not.
[Designing for exit] Keeping an abstraction in place: Keep an abstraction between application code and provider so a model swap is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

[Designing for exit] The real costs of lock-in: Understand the real costs of lock-in beyond price: model availability, feature pace, negotiating position, and the work of proving a new platform is safe.
[Moving] Migration as an evaluation exercise: Plan a migration between platforms or providers as an evaluation exercise, re-running your eval suite before, during, and after the move.
[Moving] Catalog lag & deprecation: Handle catalog lag and platform-side deprecation, since managed catalogs trail the frontier and retire versions on their own schedule.
[Moving] Running two platforms in parallel: Run two platforms in parallel where the workload justifies it, using a gateway to route by capability, region, cost, or availability.
[Moving] Multi-cloud, honestly: Understand multi-cloud honestly: it buys resilience and leverage, and it costs duplicated evaluation, duplicated security review, and duplicated operational knowledge.
Shadow traffic on the new platform: Mirror a slice of production prompts and compare quality, latency and cost before cutover.
Feature-flag the provider: Switch models and platforms from config, not from a code deploy.
Dual-run cost cap: Bound how long two platforms run in parallel and who pays for the overlap.
Deprecation runbook: List the owner, the eval gate and the rollback when a catalog version is retired.

links.title: Level 11 module M11.9: Capstone: deploy on a managed platform (source)

nodes.title: Capstone · deploy on a managed platform
nodes.summary: Ship it: the Level 11 capstone. Ship it · Level 11 capstone. Build it, publish it, and be ready to explain every decision.
checklist: Redeploy an app you already built: Take an application you built in an earlier level and redeploy it against a managed platform, keeping the behavior and changing the plumbing.
Cloud identity, no API key: Authenticate through cloud identity with least-privilege access to a named set of models, and remove the provider API key from the application entirely.
Private path & recorded data handling: Route model traffic over a private network path, and record where the data is processed, how long it is retained, and under which terms.
One component bought, one built: Replace at least one hand-built component with a managed equivalent, and keep at least one hand-built because you can defend why.
Re-run your evals after the move: Re-run your evaluation suite on the migrated system and report what changed in quality, latency, and cost.
A gateway with a working fallback: Route the application's model calls through a gateway with a working fallback, or state why direct calls to one provider are enough at your scale.
Capacity sizing & budget alert: Size capacity for your expected traffic, set a budget alert, and state the volume at which a different pricing model would win.
A platform decision record: Write a one-page platform decision record: the workload, the constraints, the path chosen, the components bought and built, and the exit plan.

nodes.title: Level 12 overview: Multimodal 101: Beyond Text
nodes.summary: Level 12 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Build a strong mental model of how models handle images, audio, and video, why they fail differently from text models, and how to choose and use the right model when a task stops being text-only.
checklist: Why it matters in interviews (4/10): Seldom asked unless the role is specifically about vision, speech, or documents. Low payoff for general applications.
Why it matters on the job (5/10): Very important in some domains (documents, speech, vision), not needed in many others.
Prerequisites: Level 1 · LLM 101  Level 2 · Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration)  Level 4 · RAG

Goal of this level: Level 12 of the CampusX AI Engineering Roadmap: Build a strong mental model of how models handle images, audio, and video, why they fail differently from text models, and how to choose and use the right model when a task stops being text-only.
Plan 12 modules and the capstone “ship a multimodal build” before moving on

nodes.title: M12.1 · Beyond text: what a multimodal model is
nodes.summary: M12.1 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 8 topics: What makes a model multimodal; Native multimodal vs bolted-on pipeline; Text as the interlingua.
checklist: What makes a model multimodal: Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text.

Native multimodal vs bolted-on pipeline: Distinguish a natively multimodal model, trained on mixed data from the start, from a pipeline that bolts a separate transcription, OCR, or captioning model in front of a text-only LLM.
Text as the interlingua: Understand why text remains the interlingua: whatever enters the model, the reasoning and almost always the output happen in tokens that behave like text.
What carries over from text LLMs: Build intuition for what changes and what does not: the context window, tokenization, sampling, and failure modes you learned for text all still apply.
What "any-to-any" really means: Recognize what "any-to-any" marketing does and does not mean today, since most models accept several input modalities but produce only text.
What a pipeline throws away: Understand why a bolted-on pipeline loses information that a native model keeps, such as tone in speech or layout in a scanned page.
Shared embedding space: Text and image tokens meet in one transformer, with different encoders.
Interview: multimodal vs a pipeline: One model vs ASR-then-LLM; pick on latency, cost and error compounding.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.1: Beyond text: what a multimodal model is (source)

nodes.title: M12.2 · Vision: how images become tokens
nodes.summary: M12.2 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 8 topics: Patches & the vision encoder; Why one image costs many tokens; Tiling & detail settings.
checklist: Patches & the vision encoder: Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume.
Why one image costs many tokens: Build intuition for why a single image can cost hundreds or thousands of tokens, and why that cost scales with resolution rather than with file size.
Tiling & detail settings: Understand tiling and detail settings: high-detail modes slice a large image into multiple tiles, each priced as its own set of tokens.
What downscaling destroys: Recognize what downscaling and aspect-ratio changes destroy, especially small text, thin lines, dense tables, and fine chart labels.
Images share the context window: Understand that image tokens occupy the same context window as text tokens, so a handful of screenshots can crowd out the instructions and history around them.
Full image, crops, or overview: Understand the practical trade-off between sending one large detailed image, several cropped regions, or a downscaled overview.
Patch size and resolution: More patches cost more tokens; tiny text in an image can vanish.
Interview: why a screenshot fails: Resolution, compression, and the model reading pixels as texture.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.2: Vision: how images become tokens (source)

nodes.title: M12.3 · Vision: capabilities & failure modes
nodes.summary: M12.3 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 8 topics: What vision models do well; Counting, space & dense tables; Fabricated visual detail.
checklist: What vision models do well: Understand what vision models genuinely do well: reading text in images, describing scenes, extracting named fields from documents, and interpreting charts at a coarse level.

Counting, space & dense tables: Understand the failure modes that repeat across models: precise counting, spatial and geometric reasoning, dense small text, and exact row-to-column alignment in tables.
Fabricated visual detail: Recognize fabricated detail, where a model confidently reports values, labels, or objects that a low-resolution or ambiguous image never actually contained.
Why vision failures happen: Understand why these failures happen: the model is generating a plausible description of an image it perceives as patches, not measuring or verifying anything.
Asking "how reliably?" for images: Adopt the engineering question for vision too: not "can this model read invoices?", but "how reliably does it read my invoices, at my resolution, in my formats?".
Safeguards when reliability is short: Understand which safeguards apply when reliability is not enough, such as higher resolution, cropping, structured output, verification passes, or human review.
Hallucinated UI text: Never trust an OCR-from-pixels number without a second check.
Interview: vision failure modes: Small text, charts, and counting — say how you verify.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.3: Vision: capabilities & failure modes (source)

nodes.title: M12.4 · Vision: documents, charts & visual RAG
nodes.summary: M12.4 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 17 topics: Text-layer PDFs vs scans; OCR vs native vision reading; Layout & reading order.
checklist: [Reading a document as an image] Text-layer PDFs vs scans: Distinguish a digital PDF that carries its own text layer from a scan or photograph where every character has to be recovered from pixels.

[Reading a document as an image] OCR vs native vision reading: Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve.

[Reading a document as an image] Layout & reading order: Understand why reading order matters: multi-column pages, headers, footers, footnotes, and sidebars can turn a correct page into nonsense when flattened badly.

[Reading a document as an image] Tables, forms & merged cells: Read tables and forms reliably, including merged cells, multi-page tables, checkboxes, and key-value layouts where the label and the value sit far apart.

[Reading a document as an image] How models read charts: Understand what a model actually does with a chart: it reads axes, labels, and legends rather than the underlying numbers, so precise values are often estimated.

[Extraction into structured fields] Schema before prompt: Define the schema before the prompt: name the fields you need, their types, and which of them are required, instead of asking for a free-form summary.

[Extraction into structured fields] Extract & validate fields: Extract fields from a document with a vision model and validate the result against that schema, checking types, ranges, dates, totals, and required values.

[Extraction into structured fields] Grounding fields to page regions: Ground every extracted field in its source by returning the page number or region it came from, so a human can verify a value without rereading the document.

[Extraction into structured fields] Document failure modes: Recognize document-specific failure modes: invented values in blank cells, rows merged across page breaks, confused units or currencies, and misread handwriting.
[Extraction into structured fields] Routing low confidence to review: Route low-confidence extractions to human review rather than letting an uncertain value flow silently into a database.

[Visual RAG] Pages & regions as retrieval units: Understand what changes when the retrieval unit is a page image or a region of a page rather than a chunk of text, and how embeddings are produced for it.
[Visual RAG] Hybrid text + visual retrieval: Build hybrid retrieval that searches extracted text and page images together, and recognize which of the two wins for a given question.
[Visual RAG] Citing the page you answered from: Cite the page or region an answer came from, so the reader can open the document at the right place and check it.
[Visual RAG] When plain text beats visual: Compare a visual pipeline with a plain text pipeline on cost, latency, and accuracy, and understand why clean digital text rarely needs page images at all.
[Visual RAG] The token cost of page images: Understand the practical cost of visual RAG: page images consume far more tokens than the equivalent text, which changes both latency and price per query.
Grounded image answers: Ask for a bounding description tied to visible evidence.
When to use a dedicated OCR: Forms and invoices still want a specialist.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.4: Vision: documents, charts & visual RAG (source)

nodes.title: M12.5 · Vision: image & video generation
nodes.summary: M12.5 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 11 topics: Denoising, not next-token prediction; What a prompt controls; Seeds & reproducibility.
checklist: [How generation differs from prediction] Denoising, not next-token prediction: Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does.

[How generation differs from prediction] What a prompt controls: Understand what a prompt actually controls in image generation: subject, composition, style, and detail, with far less literal instruction-following than a text model offers.

[How generation differs from prediction] Seeds & reproducibility: Understand seeds and reproducibility: the same prompt with the same seed returns the same image, while a new seed produces a different interpretation of the same words.
[How generation differs from prediction] Resolution, steps & cost: Understand how resolution, aspect ratio, and step count affect quality, generation time, and cost.
[Control, video and rights] img2img, inpainting & outpainting: Distinguish text-to-image from image-to-image, inpainting, and outpainting, and recognize which one a given editing task actually needs.

[Control, video and rights] Style & structural control: Understand reference and style conditioning, along with structural control such as pose, depth, or edge guidance, for when a prompt alone cannot hold a layout steady.
[Control, video and rights] Cost per accepted image: Build intuition for iteration cost: generation is cheap per image but expensive per accepted image, because most candidates are discarded.

[Control, video and rights] What video adds: time & motion: Understand what video generation adds: time, motion, and consistency across frames, which makes length, cost, and failure modes grow quickly.

[Control, video and rights] Provenance, watermarks & rights: Understand provenance and rights: watermarking, content credentials, training-data licensing, and the commercial-use terms attached to generated assets.
Safety on user-uploaded images: Treat pixels as untrusted input, same as pasted text.
PII in photos: Faces and documents need a retention and redact policy.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.5: Vision: image & video generation (source)

nodes.title: M12.6 · Audio: how sound becomes tokens
nodes.summary: M12.6 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 8 topics: Waveform to spectrogram to tokens; Cost per second, not per word; Transcribe-then-prompt vs audio-native.
checklist: Waveform to spectrogram to tokens: Understand the path from a waveform to model input: audio is sampled, converted into a spectrogram or learned audio tokens, and then treated as another token stream.
Cost per second, not per word: Build intuition for audio cost and latency, where tokens accumulate per second of duration rather than per word, so silence and background noise are paid for too.
Transcribe-then-prompt vs audio-native: Distinguish transcribe-then-prompt pipelines, where a speech-to-text model produces text for an LLM, from audio-native models that consume the sound itself.
What a transcript discards: Understand what a transcript discards: tone, emphasis, hesitation, overlapping speakers, emotion, and everything that separates "fine" said warmly from "fine" said flatly.
Why audio is latency-sensitive: Recognize why audio input and output are latency-sensitive, since a conversation is judged on response delay in a way that a document summary never is.
Where speech recognition breaks: Understand common audio failure modes such as accented speech, code-switching between languages, domain jargon, poor microphones, and long silences.
Streaming ASR vs batch: Live captions need a different latency budget than a podcast transcript.
Interview: audio token path: Waveform to patches or to text first — and what errors each adds.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.6: Audio: how sound becomes tokens (source)

nodes.title: M12.7 · Audio: speech to text & text to speech
nodes.summary: M12.7 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 12 topics: What Whisper actually returns; Batch vs streaming transcription; Accents, code-mixing & noise.
checklist: [Speech to text] What Whisper actually returns: Understand what a speech-to-text model such as Whisper produces: a transcript, optional word timestamps, and confidence signals rather than clean edited prose.

[Speech to text] Batch vs streaming transcription: Distinguish batch transcription of a complete recording from streaming transcription, where partial text is emitted while the speaker is still talking.

[Speech to text] Accents, code-mixing & noise: Understand what degrades transcription in practice — accents, code-mixed Hindi-English speech, background noise, and poor microphones — and supply domain vocabulary as hints.
[Speech to text] Speaker diarization: Use speaker diarization to attribute each segment to a speaker, and understand why it is a separate step that fails in its own ways.
[Speech to text] Word error rate in practice: Read word error rate as a measure of transcription quality, and reason about which errors actually matter for whatever happens downstream.

[Text to speech] What Kokoro turns text into: Understand what a text-to-speech model such as Kokoro turns text into: sampled audio in a chosen voice, produced in one pass or streamed as it is generated.
[Text to speech] Voice choice & prosody: Choose a voice and shape prosody through pace, pauses, and emphasis, and understand how much control a given model actually exposes.
[Text to speech] Pronunciation control: Control the pronunciation of names, acronyms, numbers, and code-mixed text, since these are where synthetic speech usually embarrasses itself.
[Text to speech] Streaming synthesis: Stream synthesis so the first audio reaches the listener while the rest is still being generated, instead of waiting for the whole utterance.
[Text to speech] Hosted vs local speech models: Compare hosted and locally run speech models on cost, latency, privacy, and voice quality, and choose per workload rather than by default.
Speaker and noise robustness: A demo in a quiet room is not production.
Transcript as the interface: Most products still want text they can search and eval.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.7: Audio: speech to text & text to speech (source)

nodes.title: M12.8 · Audio: realtime voice agents
nodes.summary: M12.8 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 17 topics: Latency as the design constraint; Where the milliseconds go; Cascaded vs speech-to-speech.
checklist: [The latency budget] Latency as the design constraint: Understand why a voice conversation feels broken above roughly a second of silence, and treat end-to-end latency as the primary design constraint.
[The latency budget] Where the milliseconds go: Break the latency budget into its parts: capture, network, transcription, model thinking, synthesis, and playback.

[The latency budget] Cascaded vs speech-to-speech: Distinguish a cascaded pipeline, where speech-to-text, an LLM, and text-to-speech run in sequence, from a speech-to-speech realtime API that takes audio in and returns audio.
[The latency budget] Comparing the two architectures: Compare the two architectures on latency, control, cost, debuggability, and how much of the conversation you can inspect afterwards.
[The latency budget] What can overlap: Understand which parts can overlap: synthesis can begin before the model has finished, and transcription can run while the user is still speaking.
[Turn-taking] Voice activity detection & endpointing: Understand voice activity detection and endpointing as the mechanism that decides when the user has actually stopped speaking.
[Turn-taking] Why endpointing is hard: Recognize why endpointing is hard: pauses for thought, slow speakers, and background chatter all look like the end of a turn.
[Turn-taking] Barge-in & interruption: Handle barge-in, where the user interrupts mid-answer, by stopping playback and discarding the rest of the planned response.
[Turn-taking] Acting on partial transcripts: Use partial transcripts to start work early, and understand the risk of acting on text the user has not finished saying.
[Turn-taking] State after a cut-short turn: Keep conversation state consistent when a turn is cut short, so the model does not believe it said something the user never heard.
[Failure, noise & tools] Silence, dead air & dropped calls: Handle silence, dead air, and network loss with holding phrases, reconnection, and a graceful exit rather than an unexplained pause.
[Failure, noise & tools] Noise, crosstalk & bad mics: Understand what background noise, crosstalk, and poor microphones do to a live pipeline, and where to place the safeguards.
[Failure, noise & tools] Staying alive during tool calls: Keep the conversation alive while a tool call runs, since a lookup that takes three seconds is silence the user will not tolerate.
[Failure, noise & tools] What to say while waiting: Decide what the agent says while it waits, and what it does when the tool fails or returns nothing useful.
[Failure, noise & tools] Reconstructing a bad call: Capture what a voice session needs for later reconstruction: audio, transcript, timings, and turn boundaries.
Voice output is another model: TTS quality and latency are separate SLOs.
Barge-in and interrupts: Users talk over the bot; the pipeline must cancel.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.8: Audio: realtime voice agents (source)

nodes.title: M12.9 · Cross-modal search & retrieval
nodes.summary: M12.9 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 8 topics: A shared embedding space; CLIP-style joint embeddings; Searching across modalities.
checklist: A shared embedding space: Understand a shared embedding space, where an image and a caption that describe the same thing land close together as vectors.
CLIP-style joint embeddings: Understand CLIP-style joint embeddings, where two encoders are trained so that matching image-text pairs are pulled together and mismatched pairs pushed apart.
Searching across modalities: Search images with a text query and search text with an image query, using the same vector-search machinery Level 4 introduced for text.
Cross-modal vs caption-then-search: Distinguish cross-modal retrieval from captioning every image first and searching the captions, and recognize when each approach wins.
Where cross-modal retrieval fails: Recognize where cross-modal retrieval fails: fine-grained detail, text inside images, counting, and domain-specific imagery the encoder never saw.
Evaluating on your own collection: Evaluate retrieval quality on your own images and queries rather than trusting a benchmark score measured on a general image collection.
Image-to-text retrieval: Caption then search vs native multimodal embed — measure both.
Interview: cross-modal search: Query type, index type, and the metric you refuse to mix.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.9: Cross-modal search & retrieval (source)

nodes.title: M12.10 · Choosing a multimodal model
nodes.summary: M12.10 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 10 topics: Start from the modalities; Per-image & per-minute pricing; The context cost of images.
checklist: Start from the modalities: Start from the modalities themselves: list what must go in, whether text, images, audio, video, or documents, and what must come out.
Per-image & per-minute pricing: Understand how multimodal pricing works, since per-image and per-audio-minute charges sit alongside per-token pricing and cost stops being about text length alone.
The context cost of images: Understand the context cost of images, where a single image consumes a large, resolution-dependent share of the context window and limits how many you can pass at once.
Latency by modality: Compare latency expectations by modality, including time to first audio for streaming voice, where a delay is heard by the user rather than merely measured.
API vs self-hosting: Weigh API access against self-hosting for vision and speech, where open models are strong and per-minute costs at volume can outgrow the operational effort.
Privacy for voice, faces & scans: Treat privacy as a harder constraint here, because voices, faces, and scanned documents carry consent and data-residency obligations that plain text often does not.

Managed speech, vision & document services: Consider managed speech, vision, and document services from the cloud platforms alongside general multimodal models, since a narrow managed service is often cheaper and more accurate at one job.
Shortlist, then test your own data: Shortlist two or three candidates, then test them on your own images, recordings, and documents before committing, exactly as you would for a text model.
Eval sets need the media: A text-only golden set will not catch a vision miss.
Human review for safety: Automated judges miss sexual or violent imagery more than they miss grammar.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.10: Choosing a multimodal model (source)

nodes.title: M12.11 · Deep research & long-horizon scenarios
nodes.summary: M12.11 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 12 topics: Why long runs are different; Decomposing a research question; Breadth first, then depth.
checklist: [Planning a long run] Why long runs are different: Understand what changes when a task runs for many minutes across many sources instead of resolving inside a single prompt and a single response.

[Planning a long run] Decomposing a research question: Decompose a research question into sub-questions that can be investigated independently, and recognize when a question is too vague to decompose yet.
[Planning a long run] Breadth first, then depth: Search broadly before going deep: gather many candidate sources first, judge which few are worth reading closely, and discard the rest deliberately.

[Planning a long run] Reading sources critically: Read sources critically rather than accumulating them, distinguishing primary evidence, secondary commentary, marketing material, and outdated claims.

[Planning a long run] Reconciling disagreement: Reconcile sources that disagree by preferring better evidence, stating the disagreement explicitly, or reporting genuine uncertainty instead of averaging the answers.
[Finishing a long run] Claims attached to sources: Keep every claim attached to the source it came from, so a reader can verify any individual statement without repeating the whole search.

[Finishing a long run] Notes and interim summaries: Manage a run that outlives its context by writing notes and interim summaries as the work proceeds, and by carrying forward findings rather than raw source text.

[Finishing a long run] Knowing when to stop: Recognize the stopping conditions of a research run: the question is answered, the sources have started repeating, or the remaining uncertainty cannot be resolved by more searching.

[Finishing a long run] A report a human can audit: Produce a structured report a human can audit, with the question, the answer, the supporting evidence, the contradictions found, and the gaps that remain.

[Finishing a long run] How long runs fail: Understand the characteristic failures of long-horizon runs: drifting away from the original question, confident synthesis of thin evidence, and citations that do not support the sentence attached to them.
Cost of pixels and seconds: Images and audio dwarf text tokens; cache and downscale first.
A cheaper cascade: Small classifier, then the multimodal model only when needed.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.11: Deep research & long-horizon scenarios (source)

nodes.title: M12.12 · Capstone: ship a multimodal build
nodes.summary: M12.12 in L12 · Multimodal 101: Beyond Text, 7 topics: Why modalities suit the device; Quantization & what it costs; Phone & laptop hardware limits.
checklist: Why modalities suit the device: Understand why speech and vision suit on-device execution, since the models are small, the input is private, and the network round trip is often the slowest part.
Quantization & what it costs: Understand quantization as trading numerical precision for size and speed, and recognize the tasks where that trade shows up first as degraded quality.
Phone & laptop hardware limits: Build intuition for hardware limits on phones and laptops, including memory ceilings, thermal throttling, and battery cost during sustained inference.
What on-device buys you: Understand what on-device execution buys you: offline operation, no per-request cost, predictable latency, and data that never leaves the user's machine.
On-device, self-hosted or API: Choose deliberately between on-device, self-hosted, and API execution for each modality, since one application can reasonably use all three at once.
The multimodal capstone contract: Input types, failure, cost, and how you eval each modality.
What you would cut: Drop a modality before you drop grounding.

links.title: Level 12 module M12.12: Capstone: ship a multimodal build (source)

nodes.title: Capstone · ship a multimodal build
nodes.summary: Ship it: the Level 12 capstone. Ship it · Level 12 capstone. Build it, publish it, and be ready to explain every decision.
checklist: Pick one realistic build: Choose one realistic build and take it all the way: a voice agent, a document-understanding pipeline, a visual search tool, or a research-report generator.
At least two modalities: Combine at least two modalities in a single application so the build exercises a real cross-modal boundary rather than one model in isolation.
Real inputs, not samples: Feed the system real inputs from your own domain, including the messy scans, accented speech, and awkward layouts that curated sample files never contain.

Modality-specific failures: Handle the modality-specific failures your build will actually hit, such as unreadable regions, silence and background noise, hallucinated chart values, or ambiguous references.
Latency and cost per request: Measure latency and cost per request, and report them broken down by modality so the expensive part of the pipeline is visible.
Document one real failure: Document one failure you found by testing on real inputs, explaining what broke, how you detected it, and what you changed in response.
Runnable by someone else: Package the build so another person can run it from a README with their own inputs, their own credentials, and no help from you.

nodes.title: M13.1 · Should you fine-tune?
nodes.summary: M13.1 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 10 topics: Fine-tuning as the costliest option; What fine-tuning is good for; What it is not good for.
checklist: Fine-tuning as the costliest option: Decide between a better prompt, retrieval, tool use, a stronger base model, fine-tuning, or a combination, and treat fine-tuning as the most expensive option on that list.

What fine-tuning is good for: Understand what fine-tuning is good for: consistent behavior and style, output formats a prompt cannot hold, narrow structured tasks, shorter prompts, and specializing a smaller model.

What it is not good for: Understand what fine-tuning is usually not good for: teaching facts that change, which retrieval can supply fresh, and fixing a task nobody has yet defined well enough to evaluate.
Start from a measured failure: Start from a named failure mode: the prompted system fails a specific, measured way, and the failure persists after reasonable prompt and retrieval work.
The full cost of a tune: Estimate the full cost before starting, including data creation, training runs, evaluation, serving the tuned model, and retraining when the base model is replaced.
Tied to one base model: Understand that a fine-tune ties you to one base model version, so a better base model next quarter means repeating the work rather than changing a model name.
Prompt then retrieve then tune: Exhaust prompt and retrieval fixes and write the residual error before opening a training job.
Style versus knowledge test: Classify the failure as format or tone versus missing facts; only the first is a tune candidate.
Retrain tax in the estimate: Include the next base-model upgrade in the cost, not only the first run.
Decline a tune in an interview: Be ready to tell a hiring manager why you would not fine-tune their FAQ bot.

nodes.title: M13.2 · Data curation for fine-tuning
nodes.summary: M13.2 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 14 topics: Specify the behavior first; Where examples come from; Match the chat template.
checklist: [Sourcing and formatting examples] Specify the behavior first: Define the behavior you want in writing before collecting data, so every example can be checked against the same specification.

[Sourcing and formatting examples] Where examples come from: Source examples from real usage logs, expert-written demonstrations, or carefully filtered synthetic data, and understand the bias each source brings.

[Sourcing and formatting examples] Match the chat template: Format examples in the chat template the base model was trained with, since a mismatched template silently degrades the tune and the model that serves it.

[Sourcing and formatting examples] Loss on responses, not prompts: Decide what the model should learn from each example, and mask the loss so training targets the assistant's responses rather than the prompts.
[Sourcing and formatting examples] Few clean beats many noisy: Understand why a few hundred clean, representative examples often beat thousands of noisy ones for a narrow task.
[Cleaning, balancing and splitting] Cleaning bad examples: Remove duplicates, contradictions, wrong labels, truncated responses, and synthetic examples that repeat the same phrasing.
[Cleaning, balancing and splitting] Balancing edge cases: Balance common cases with the difficult and important edge cases, so the model does not learn that the easy path is always right.
[Cleaning, balancing and splitting] Leak-free splits: Split data into training, validation, and held-out test sets, and keep near-duplicates from leaking across the split.
[Cleaning, balancing and splitting] PII & licensed content: Check the data for personal information, licensed content, and anything you would not want a model to repeat word for word.
[Cleaning, balancing and splitting] Versioning the dataset: Version the dataset alongside the training configuration, so every tuned model can be traced back to exactly what it learned from.
Gold-spec before collection: Write acceptance rules an example must pass, then reject logs that miss them.
Near-duplicate leak scan: Hash normalized prompts so a paraphrase of a test item never lands in train.
Synthetic diversity checks: Measure n-gram overlap across teacher-written examples and drop clones.
Label audit sample: Hand-review a fixed 50-row sample every dataset version and record the error rate.

links.title: Level 13 module M13.2: Data curation for fine-tuning (source)

nodes.title: M13.3 · Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
nodes.summary: M13.3 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 12 topics: What SFT changes; Hyperparameters that matter; Full vs parameter-efficient.
checklist: [The training loop] What SFT changes: Understand how supervised fine-tuning nudges a pretrained or instruction-tuned model toward labelled examples by minimizing loss on the target responses.
[The training loop] Hyperparameters that matter: Learn the hyperparameters that matter first: learning rate, epochs, batch size, sequence length, and gradient accumulation.
[The training loop] Full vs parameter-efficient: Understand full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient methods, and why updating every weight is rarely necessary for a narrow task.
[The training loop] A first SFT run with TRL: Run a small SFT job with a library such as TRL and confirm that the loss falls on both training and validation data.
[Reading the run] Reading the loss curves: Read training and validation curves to recognize underfitting, overfitting, and an unstable run that needs a lower learning rate.
[Reading the run] Catastrophic forgetting: Recognize catastrophic forgetting, where the model gains the narrow skill and loses general abilities it had before.
[Reading the run] Read outputs, not just loss: Inspect sample outputs at each checkpoint rather than trusting the loss curve alone, since a lower loss does not guarantee better answers.
[Reading the run] Choosing a checkpoint: Choose the checkpoint to keep from validation behavior, not from whichever epoch happened to finish last.
Learning-rate sweep first: Try a small learning-rate grid before changing epochs or architecture.
Early-stop on the skill, not the loss: Stop when the task metric plateaus even if loss still falls.
Forgetting probe set: Keep a small general-ability set and fail the run if it drops past a threshold.
Reproducible SFT config: Pin seed, dataset hash, template and package versions in the run file.

nodes.title: M13.4 · LoRA & QLoRA
nodes.summary: M13.4 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 12 topics: LoRA adapters; QLoRA on a quantized base; Rank, alpha & target modules.
checklist: [How adapters work] LoRA adapters: Understand LoRA as freezing the base model and training small low-rank adapter matrices that are added to selected layers.
[How adapters work] QLoRA on a quantized base: Understand QLoRA as loading the frozen base model in quantized form so the same tune fits on a much smaller GPU.
[How adapters work] Rank, alpha & target modules: Reason about the settings that matter: rank, alpha, target modules, dropout, precision, and quantization type.
[How adapters work] Adapters vs full fine-tuning: Understand the trade-off between adapter-based tuning and full-model fine-tuning on quality, memory, training time, and storage.
[Running a tune on one GPU] PEFT with Unsloth or Axolotl: Fine-tune an open-weight model with PEFT through tooling such as Unsloth or Axolotl, using a configuration file you can rerun exactly.
[Running a tune on one GPU] Estimating GPU memory: Estimate GPU memory from parameter count, precision, sequence length, and batch size before renting hardware.
[Running a tune on one GPU] Tracking runs: Track each run with its dataset version, configuration, and evaluation results so experiments can be compared rather than remembered.

[Running a tune on one GPU] DIY vs managed fine-tuning: Compare running the tune yourself with a managed fine-tuning service, including which base models it offers and whether you can take the weights away.
Rank versus quality curve: Sweep rank on a held-out set and pick the smallest rank that holds the gain.
Which layers to adapt: Start with attention projections; add MLP only if the eval still misses.
Merge versus keep-separate: Know when to merge for a single deploy and when to keep adapters swappable.
QLoRA precision traps: Re-evaluate after dequantizing for serve; a 4-bit train does not guarantee a 4-bit win.

nodes.title: M13.5 · Preference tuning & DPO
nodes.summary: M13.5 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 12 topics: Demonstrations vs preferences; Building preference pairs; Sources & rater agreement.
checklist: [Preference data] Demonstrations vs preferences: Understand the difference between demonstration data, which shows one correct answer, and preference data, which says that one answer is better than another.
[Preference data] Building preference pairs: Create preference examples containing a prompt, a preferred response, and a rejected response that differ in the quality you care about.
[Preference data] Sources & rater agreement: Collect preferences from human raters, from your own eval judges, or from production feedback, and check how often raters agree with each other.
[Preference data] Avoiding length bias: Avoid preference pairs that differ in irrelevant ways, such as length, which teach the model the wrong lesson.

[Running DPO] DPO intuition: Understand the intuition behind Direct Preference Optimization without reinforcement-learning mathematics: raise the likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones.
[Running DPO] DPO after SFT: Run DPO on top of an SFT checkpoint, and understand why preference tuning usually follows supervised tuning rather than replacing it.
[Running DPO] What preference tuning is for: Use preference tuning for qualities that are hard to write as a single correct answer, such as tone, helpfulness, refusal behavior, or concision.
[Running DPO] When SFT is enough: Know when SFT alone is sufficient and when preference optimization adds measurable value.
Pair construction rules: Make preferred and rejected differ only on the quality you named.
Inter-rater agreement: Measure rater agreement and pause labeling if it stays near chance.
Beta and reference model: Know what the DPO beta does and why you need a frozen reference.
Preference versus SFT A/B: Ship DPO only when it beats the SFT checkpoint on the same held-out pairs.

nodes.title: M13.6 · Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT)
nodes.summary: M13.6 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 10 topics: Reward-based tuning; RFT vs SFT vs DPO; Tasks with gradable outputs.
checklist: Reward-based tuning: Understand reward-based fine-tuning, where the model's outputs are scored and training pushes it toward higher-scoring behavior.
RFT vs SFT vs DPO: Distinguish RFT from SFT and preference optimization by what each one learns from: examples, comparisons, or a reward.

Tasks with gradable outputs: Identify tasks suited to RFT, where outputs can be graded reliably and automatically, such as code that must pass tests, math with checkable answers, or structured outputs with verifiable fields.
Reward design & reward hacking: Understand reward design as the hard part, and recognize reward hacking, where the model optimizes the grader instead of the real objective.
Reaching RFT in practice: Understand why RFT is usually reached through a managed service or a specialized framework rather than built from scratch.
Verifiable reward only: Use RFT when a checker, test suite or schema can score the output without a human.
Reward-hacking gallery: Collect cases where the model pads, repeats or games the grader and add them to the suite.
KL or length penalty: Bound how far the policy may drift from the SFT reference.
Rubric versus unit-test rewards: Prefer machine-checkable scores; use a rubric judge only when a test cannot exist.
When not to reach for RL: Skip RFT if you cannot write a grader you trust more than a preference pair.

nodes.title: M13.7 · Distillation
nodes.summary: M13.7 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 10 topics: Teacher → student; Generating & filtering teacher outputs; Capability for cost & latency.
checklist: Teacher → student: Understand teacher-to-student distillation: a stronger model produces outputs that train a smaller model for one narrow workload.
Generating & filtering teacher outputs: Generate teacher outputs on inputs that resemble real traffic, and filter them with your evals before they become training data.
Capability for cost & latency: Use distillation to trade a small amount of capability for lower cost, lower latency, and a model you can host yourself.
Copied mistakes, low diversity: Understand the risks of copying teacher mistakes and of low-diversity synthetic data that narrows what the student can handle.
Teacher terms of use: Check the teacher model's terms of use, since some providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models.
On-policy student inputs: Distill on prompts from real traffic, not only the teacher's favorite demos.
Filter then train: Drop teacher rows that fail your evals before they become the student's truth.
Student-versus-teacher gap: Report quality, latency and cost of both models on the same set.
Licence of teacher outputs: Confirm the teacher API allows training a competing or replacement model.
Distill versus buy a smaller API: Compare a distilled self-hosted student with the teacher's cheap small-model SKU.

nodes.title: M13.8 · Evaluating fine-tunes
nodes.summary: M13.8 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 11 topics: Baselines before training; Same held-out set, same judge; Beyond a single score.
checklist: [Baselines and the held-out test] Baselines before training: Establish the baselines before training: the base model, the best prompted version of it, and a stronger model with the same prompt.

[Baselines and the held-out test] Same held-out set, same judge: Evaluate every candidate on the same held-out test set with the Level 7 evaluation framework, using the same metrics and the same judge.
[Baselines and the held-out test] Beyond a single score: Compare quality, latency, cost per request, output consistency, and specific failure cases rather than a single aggregate score.

[Regressions and the decision] Regressions outside the task: Check for regressions outside the narrow capability you tuned, including general instruction-following, safety behavior, and formats the tune never saw.
[Regressions and the decision] Reading individual failures: Read individual failures from the tuned model, since an average improvement can hide a new failure the base model never had.
[Regressions and the decision] Simpler alternatives, one last time: Compare against simpler alternatives one final time, and accept the result when a better prompt or a stronger base model wins.
[Regressions and the decision] Writing the decision down: Write the decision down: what improved, by how much, what regressed, and whether the gain justifies serving and maintaining the tune.
Slice metrics, not only mean: Break scores by language, length, tool-use and the original failure mode.
Safety and format probes: Re-run refusal and schema tests after every tune, even if the task is unrelated.
Cost-normalized quality: Report quality per dollar and per second, not quality alone.
Kill-criteria in writing: Pre-commit the regression that would reject the tune before you see the numbers.

nodes.title: M13.9 · Capstone: a LoRA that beats a prompted baseline
nodes.summary: M13.9 in Level 13 (Fine-Tuning), 14 topics: Separate adapter or merged weights; Save, load & merge; Multi-LoRA serving with vLLM.
checklist: [Getting the tune into production] Separate adapter or merged weights: Choose between keeping a LoRA adapter separate from the base model and merging it into the weights, and understand what each choice means for storage, loading, and swapping.
[Getting the tune into production] Save, load & merge: Save, load, and merge adapters, and confirm that the merged model reproduces the adapter's evaluation results.
[Getting the tune into production] Multi-LoRA serving with vLLM: Serve the base model with one or several adapters through vLLM, where many adapters can share one base model on the same GPU.

[Getting the tune into production] Quantized export for Ollama: Export the tuned model to a quantized format for local runtimes such as Ollama, and re-run evaluation after quantization, since it can undo part of the gain.

[Getting the tune into production] Managed & serverless adapter hosting: Host an adapter on a managed platform or a serverless inference provider that serves adapters on shared base models, and compare that with running your own GPU.

[Owning it in production] Matching template & tokenizer: Serve with exactly the chat template and tokenizer used in training, since a template mismatch is the most common reason a good tune behaves badly in production.
[Owning it in production] Versioning & rollback: Version the adapter, base model, dataset, and configuration together, and keep the previous version deployable for rollback.

[Owning it in production] Gradual rollout via the gateway: Route traffic between the base model and the tuned model through your gateway, and roll the tune out gradually while watching evaluation and production metrics.
[Owning it in production] Latency & cost vs baseline: Measure latency and cost per request for the served tune and compare them with the prompted baseline the tune replaced.

[Owning it in production] Retraining triggers: Plan for retraining: decide what triggers it, such as a new base model, drifting inputs, or new failure cases, and how the eval suite gates each new version.
Adapter id in every trace: Log base model, adapter version and template so a bad answer is reproducible.
Canary then promote: Send a small slice of traffic to the new adapter and promote only if eval and error rate hold.
Template mismatch drill: Serve the tune with the wrong template once in staging and record the failure shape.
Retrain trigger SLI: Name the metric and window (new base model, drift, new failures) that opens a training job.

nodes.title: Capstone · a LoRA that beats a prompted baseline
nodes.summary: Ship it: the Level 13 capstone. Ship it · Level 13 capstone. Build it, publish it, and be ready to explain every decision.
checklist: A narrow task with a measured failure: Choose one narrow, real task where the best prompt you can write still fails in a way you can measure.
Metric & threshold up front: Write down the failure, the metric that will judge success, and the threshold the tune must clear before any training starts.
A strong prompted baseline: Build the strongest prompted baseline you can, including few-shot examples and retrieval where relevant, and record its score on a held-out test set.
Clean, leak-free dataset: Create a clean, versioned dataset with training, validation, and held-out splits that do not leak into each other.
Reproducible LoRA/QLoRA run: Run an SFT tune with LoRA or QLoRA from a configuration file someone else can rerun, and add preference tuning only if the evaluation shows a gap it can close.
Same-set comparison & cost: Evaluate the tuned and prompted models on the same held-out set, and report quality, latency, tokens per request, and cost per thousand requests.
Regressions & one failure: Test for regressions on prompts outside the target task, and document at least one failure the tune introduced or failed to fix.
Serve it, reproduce the numbers: Serve the adapter behind an endpoint with the correct chat template, and confirm the served model reproduces the offline evaluation numbers.
A fine-tuning decision record: Write a one-page fine-tuning decision record: the failure, the data, the configuration, the before-and-after numbers, the cost to serve, and the retraining trigger.

nodes.summary: M15.5 in L15 · GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep, 8 topics: Diagnosing production incidents; Latency spikes, outages & cost explosions; Fallbacks, retries & autoscaling.
checklist: Diagnosing production incidents: Diagnose production incidents involving model APIs, self-hosted inference, retrieval services, queues, caches, rate limits, and downstream tools.
Latency spikes, outages & cost explosions: Reason through latency spikes, provider outages, cost explosions, capacity limits, and degraded model quality.
Fallbacks, retries & autoscaling: Discuss fallback strategies, graceful degradation, retries, load balancing, and autoscaling.
Reading monitoring signals: Interpret monitoring signals such as latency, throughput, error rates, token usage, cost, retrieval quality, and eval scores.
Alert, rollback or investigate: Explain what should trigger an alert and what requires rollback versus investigation.
Proprietary API vs self-hosted inference: Practice comparing proprietary API deployment with self-hosted inference under realistic traffic and privacy constraints.
A production incident story: Symptom, pin, rollback, and the eval case you added.
Interview: debug a quality drop: Check pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix.

nodes.title: M15.6 · AI system-design interviews
nodes.summary: M15.6 in L15 · GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep, 22 topics: Turning ambiguity into assumptions; Simplest viable architecture first; Whiteboarding the full AI stack.
checklist: Turning ambiguity into assumptions: Practice turning an ambiguous product requirement into explicit assumptions around users, traffic, latency, quality, cost, freshness, privacy, and reliability.
Simplest viable architecture first: Start with the simplest viable architecture before introducing RAG, agents, fine-tuning, routing, caching, or complex infrastructure.
Whiteboarding the full AI stack: Whiteboard systems using the full AI stack:
Model selection & routing: model selection/routing
RAG & context: RAG and context
Tools & agents: tools/agents
Caches: caches
Databases: databases
Inference services: inference services
Observability: observability
Evals: evals
Security: security
Deployment: deployment.

Designing under enterprise constraints: Design under enterprise constraints where a public API is not allowed, and defend a managed platform or self-hosted deployment on identity, residency, capacity, and cost.
Explaining trade-offs, not naming tools: Explain every major trade-off rather than merely naming technologies.
Systems to practise: Practice system designs such as:
Enterprise support assistant: enterprise support assistant
Coding assistant: coding assistant
Research agent: research agent
Large-scale document intelligence: large-scale document intelligence system.
System-design timebox: Requirements first, then one design, then costs and eval.
What you cut under pressure: The second agent, the graph, the extra reranker.

nodes.title: M15.7 · Staying current without chasing hype
nodes.summary: M15.7 in L15 · GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep, 8 topics: A process for evaluating what is new; Capability change vs hype; Evaluating a newly released model.
checklist: A process for evaluating what is new: Build a defensible process for evaluating new models, frameworks, papers, benchmarks, and tooling.
Capability change vs hype: Separate meaningful capability/infrastructure changes from short-lived hype.
Evaluating a newly released model: Explain how you would evaluate a newly released model before replacing an existing production model.
Benchmarks → evals → controlled rollout: Use benchmarks → shortlist → custom evals → cost/latency comparison → controlled rollout rather than social-media consensus.
"How do you stay current?": Develop a strong answer to common interview questions such as “How do you stay current in GenAI?”
A weekly reading budget: One paper or post, one note in your own words, one thing you would try.
Hype filter: If there is no eval and no failure mode, it is a demo.
Interview: how you stay current: Sources, a note habit, and what you ignored last month.

nodes.title: M15.8 · Project & portfolio defense
nodes.summary: M15.8 in L15 · GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep, 15 topics: Choosing two or three projects to defend; A structure for explaining each; Problem → architecture → results.
checklist: Choosing two or three projects to defend: Prepare 2–3 major projects from the roadmap for deep technical questioning.
A structure for explaining each: Explain each project using:
Problem → architecture → results: problem → requirements → baseline → architecture → decisions → trade-offs → failures → evals → production results.
Justifying every technology choice: Be prepared to explain why you selected a particular model, retriever, agent architecture, framework, database, or deployment strategy.
Quantifying the outcome: Quantify where possible: quality scores, latency, cost/query, throughput, dataset size, traffic, or improvement over baseline.
Discussing failures openly: Discuss failures and design mistakes openly and explain what you changed as a result.
Expected follow-ups: Prepare for interviewer follow-ups such as:
"Why didn't you use RAG?": “Why didn't you use RAG?”
"Why not fine-tune?": “Why not fine-tune?”
"Why do you need an agent?": “Why do you need an agent?”
"What happens at 100× traffic?": “What happens at 100× traffic?”
"How would you halve the cost?": “How would you reduce the cost by 50%?”
"What breaks first?": “What breaks first?”
STAR-L with a real number: Situation, task, action, result, and what you learned.
Conflict stories without villains: A trade-off you owned, not a teammate you blamed.

nodes.summary: M15.9 in L15 · GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep, 8 topics: Clarity without implementation detail; Stating assumptions first; Thinking in trade-offs.
checklist: Clarity without implementation detail: Communicate technical reasoning clearly without drowning the interviewer in implementation details.
Stating assumptions first: State assumptions before solving ambiguous design questions.
Thinking in trade-offs: Think in structured trade-offs rather than jumping directly to a tool or architecture.
Revealing a design progressively: Use diagrams and whiteboards to progressively reveal a design.
Measuring instead of bluffing: When unsure, explain how you would measure, experiment, or debug rather than bluffing.
Structuring experience-based answers: Structure experience-based answers around the situation, decision, implementation, result, and lessons learned.
The mock loop: Timed answers, recorded, scored, two weakest dimensions next week.
A close: questions that show you understand their stack, not generic culture prompts.
